body:
## What

`g2o-detect-interactive-signin-anomaly` counts every `entra.signin` with
`conditional_access_status=failure`. On a live tenant that limb produced 100% of the rule's
firings over 30 days and **not one of them was a refusal**. Exclude Entra error `50097` from the
CA limb by default, and replace the tuning note with the measurement that explains why.

## The finding (live-measured, m7kni, 2026-08-10)

30 days of interactive sign-ins, all three limbs of the live tenant-local variant of this rule:

| limb | events / 30d |
| --- | --- |
| non-GB location | 0 |
| `risk_state` atRisk/confirmedCompromised | 0 |
| `conditional_access_status=failure` | 10 |

Of those 10, **6 were error `50097` "Device authentication is required"**. Pulling
`appliedConditionalAccessPolicies` from Graph for all 6 gives an identical fingerprint:

- every **enforced** policy returned `success`
- the only non-success entry was `[Report-only] Require compliant device at Home`
  (`enabledForReportingButNotEnforced`, `grants=compliantDevice`) returning `reportOnlyFailure`
- each was followed by a **success record under the same `correlation_id`, ~1 second later**

So a **report-only** grant causes Entra to stamp `conditionalAccessStatus=failure` + errorCode
50097 on a sign-in that was never blocked. The policy is in report-only mode precisely so it does
not block, and the sign-in log records it as a failure anyway.

That makes 50097 structurally incapable of representing a compromise on such a tenant, and it is
the single largest noise source in this detection.

## Why this is portable, not tenant policy

Report-only mode is the documented, recommended way to stage a Conditional Access policy, so any
tenant rolling one out generates this exact pattern. It is not an m7kni configuration quirk — it
is how Entra records report-only evaluation. That distinguishes it from the country clause, which
this repo correctly declines to ship.

## The limitation this must state rather than hide

A 50097 that is **not** followed by a success is a genuine block, and on a tenant that *enforces*
`RequireCompliantDevice` that is the normal case. Loki cannot join two records on `correlation_id`,
so **the rule cannot tell an interrupt from a block** — the same class of limitation as the
impossible-travel entry in `alerts/README.md`. The exclusion is therefore a default chosen for the
common case, and the tuning note must name the condition that reverses it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `DETECTIONS` entry for `g2o-detect-interactive-signin-anomaly` adds `f("status_error_code", "ne", "50097")` to the CA limb
- [ ] `tuning_required` rewritten: states the report-only mechanism, the correlation-id evidence, the Loki-cannot-join limitation, and the condition under which 50097 must be put back
- [ ] `description` mentions that `appliedConditionalAccessPolicies` is where the answer lives and that graph2otel does not export it
- [ ] a hunt in `HUNTS` lets an operator measure their own 50097 rate, `unblocks` this rule
- [ ] `docs/runbooks.md` section updated (false positives + remediation)
- [ ] `alerts/README.md` detections prose updated
- [ ] `make rules` regenerates `alerts/rules/g2o-detect-interactive-signin-anomaly.yaml`; `make grafana-check` passes

comments.body:
Landed in `197718b`, pushed to `main`.

All acceptance criteria met. `make check` green before commit (408 tests OK, forks check passed, golangci-lint 0 issues, build clean).

Two things worth recording beyond the issue body:

**The hunt ships at a 14-day window, not 30.** While validating the generated query I found that a `[30d]` `count_over_time` on `{service_name="graph2otel"}` returns **empty rather than erroring** on Grafana Cloud Loki — measured on the m7kni stack 2026-08-10, `[7d]`/`[14d]`/`[21d]` all returned data and `[30d]` returned nothing on the same stream. An empty hunt result is indistinguishable from a clean tenant, which is the specific failure mode `docs/hunting.md` exists to avoid, so the new hunt uses 14d and both it and the `tuning_required` note say why.

**This affects an existing hunt too, and I have NOT touched it.** `Which risk detection types does Identity Protection raise here` also uses `window="30d"` and returned 0 series on this stack. That is inconclusive on its own — this tenant produces no Identity Protection risk detections at all, so the empty result has a second, innocent explanation. Worth a separate issue to sweep every 30d hunt against a backend that actually holds data at that range; out of scope here.

Verification that the shipped query works, run against live data:

```
50097  Azure Portal = 2
50097  Google Workspace = 2
50097  Microsoft 365 Admin portal = 1
50097  Microsoft 365 Security and Compliance Center = 1
50097  homelab-arcane = 1
50097  homelab-oauth2-proxy = 1
50097  PH OTEL = 1
50074  PH OTEL = 1
500121 PH OTEL = 1
53003  Google Workspace = 1
```

8 of 10 CA failures are 50097, which is the share the exclusion removes.

title: Detection: exclude Entra 50097 from the CA-failure limb of g2o-detect-interactive-signin-anomaly

body:
## Summary

Every blob collector re-lists its Azure Storage container on a **5-minute** cadence, declared as **eleven separate copies of `5 * time.Minute`** across eleven files. Each `ListBlobs` is a billed transaction, and at that rate the listing itself is a measurable share of the storage bill — for no latency benefit, because the delivery floor is Azure-side.

`defender.go` already states the rationale for why polling faster is pointless, and then the constant contradicts it by being as low as it is:

> `// Interval is how often each Defender container is re-listed. Records land minutes behind the event and the floor is Azure-side, so polling faster only bills list operations (#89) — the same 5-minute cadence every blob collector uses.`

The comment is right; 5 minutes is just an unexamined default. Azure Monitor writes hour-partitioned blobs and appends to the current hour on its own cadence, and blob-derived records have been measured at **3.3–7.0 days** of event-time lag on this pipeline (#297). Against that, the difference between a 5-minute and a 15-minute list is not observable in the data — it is only observable on the bill, where it is a straight 3x.

## Why one shared constant

The eleven copies are not eleven decisions. They are one decision copy-pasted, and the value is identical in all eleven:

| file | const |
| --- | --- |
| `internal/collectors/defender/defender.go` | `Interval` (covers all 24 advanced-hunting tables) |
| `internal/collectors/entra/signins/blob.go` | `blobInterval` |
| `internal/collectors/entra/directoryaudits/blob.go` | `blobInterval` |
| `internal/collectors/entra/provisioning/blob.go` | `blobInterval` |
| `internal/collectors/entra/riskdetections/blob.go` | `blobInterval` |
| `internal/collectors/entra/risk/blob.go` | `blobInterval` |
| `internal/collectors/entra/graphactivity/graphactivity.go` | `interval` |
| `internal/collectors/entra/graphnotifications/graphnotifications.go` | `interval` |
| `internal/collectors/intune/manageddevices/blob.go` | `blobInterval` |
| `internal/collectors/intune/cloudpcaudit/cloudpcaudit.go` | `blobInterval` |
| `internal/collectors/intune/compliancealerts/compliancealerts.go` | `interval` |

The polling cadence of a byte-offset blob consumer is a property of **the engine that does the listing**, not of the collector that happens to sit on it — the cost and the Azure-side latency floor are identical for all of them. So the constant belongs in `internal/blobpipeline`, where the `ListBlobs` call actually is, and where the rationale can be stated once instead of eleven times (currently it is stated properly in exactly one of the eleven).

This is deliberately **not** a config knob. The per-collector `interval:` override already exists for anyone who wants a different cadence; what is missing is a sane default and a single place to reason about it.

## Scope

- Add `blobpipeline.DefaultInterval = 15 * time.Minute`, documenting the Azure-side latency floor and the billed-listing tradeoff.
- Point all eleven collectors at it; delete the duplicated constants.
- Leave every non-blob interval alone. Window pollers hitting Graph have a completely different cost model (client-side rate limiters, throttle budgets) and are out of scope here.

## Non-goals

Not a change to `SafetyLag`, overlap windows, or any Graph poll cadence. Not a new config key.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `blobpipeline.DefaultInterval` exists and carries the rationale.
- [ ] All eleven duplicated constants are gone; no `5 * time.Minute` remains on a blob-listing path.
- [ ] A test pins that every registered blob collector reports the shared default, so a twelfth collector cannot quietly reintroduce a private copy.
- [ ] `make check` green.

comments.body:
## Two body claims reversed — recording the decisions before the commit lands

### 1. It IS a config knob after all

The body said *"This is deliberately not a config knob. The per-collector `interval:` override already exists."* The mechanism claim is correct — `CollectorSettings` does resolve a per-collector interval for blob collectors — but the conclusion does not follow. Changing the cadence globally would mean naming ~35 collectors individually, which is not a knob anyone would use.

Adding `blob_ingest.interval`, per-tenant, next to `account_url` and `metric_recency_window` — that struct already establishes exactly this shape, so it is the symmetric home rather than a new pattern. `blob_ingest` is a file-only key with no env mapping, so there is no env-var registry entry to add.

Precedence, loosest to tightest: `blobpipeline.DefaultInterval` (15m) → `blob_ingest.interval` → `collectors.<name>.interval`.

### 2. Not all eleven take the shared default — two are pinned faster, and this was nearly a silent bug

The body scoped this as "point all eleven at it". That would have broken metrics.

Exactly **two** blob collectors set `ContainerConfig.Derive` and therefore emit metrics at all: `entra.graph_activity` and the `entra.signins.*` blob streams. The other ~33 are log-only. For those two the tick is an **input to the #128 metric-recency gate**, and nothing enforced the relationship — `DefaultMetricRecencyWindow`'s own docstring derives its value from *"the tick is 5m"*:

> `// Default 20m — steady-state blob latency is ~5m and the tick is 5m, so ~15m is the floor; 20m gives margin.`

`Derive` runs only for records inside the window; older ones take the log path only. A record appended just after a tick is not read until the next, so its age at the gate is up to `tick + Azure write latency`:

| tick | worst-case age at gate | vs the 20m window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5m | ~10m | comfortable margin |
| 15m | ~20m | level with it — no margin |

At 15m the tail of every tick's batch stops counting toward metrics. **Silently**: the logs stay complete, so nothing looks broken while those two metric streams undercount.

Raising the window to compensate was considered and rejected — it re-admits older backfill into cumulative counters, which is the precise bug #128 exists to prevent. So the two are pinned to `blobpipeline.MetricDerivingInterval` (5m), `blob_ingest.interval` does not move them, and the per-collector override remains the way to change them deliberately. Cost: 2 of ~35 collectors keep the faster cadence; the remaining ~33, including all 24 Defender tables, get the 3x listing reduction.

### The gate keys on the reason, not on names

`TestBlobIntervalMatchesWhetherTheCollectorDerivesMetrics` asserts off a new `BlobCollector.DerivesMetrics()` accessor, so adding `Derive` to a log-only collector fails the build rather than quietly gating its new metrics away. A hardcoded two-name list would go stale the moment a twelfth collector lands — and the failure it guards against is invisible in production, which is exactly when a stale gate is worst.

Both gates were sabotage-checked in both directions: putting a metric collector on the slow default fails, and making a log-only collector ignore the config knob fails (48 failures, 24 Defender tables x 2 tests).

### Revised acceptance criteria

- [x] `blobpipeline.DefaultInterval` (15m) exists and carries the rationale.
- [x] `blobpipeline.MetricDerivingInterval` (5m) exists and carries the #128 arithmetic.
- [x] All eleven duplicated constants gone; no `5 * time.Minute` on a blob-listing path.
- [x] `blob_ingest.interval` added, validated, documented.
- [x] Gate keys on `DerivesMetrics()`, both halves asserted, sabotage-checked.
- [x] `docs/blob-ingest.md` documents the cadence, the precedence table and the metric-deriving exemption.
- [ ] `make check` green.

title: Blob collectors re-list every 5 minutes from 11 duplicated constants; the listing is billed and buys no freshness

body:
## Summary

[#417](https://github.com/rknightion/graph2otel/issues/417) livelocked eight collectors for **11 days** on m7kni while every health signal read green. That code bug is fixed (c47ee47). **The detection gap is not.** A different bug with the same shape would be equally invisible today.

## The three alerts that should have caught it, and why none could

Measured against the live m7kni series covering the freeze window:

| rule | fires when | actual value over the freeze |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `g2o-collector-staleness` | `scrape_staleness / expected_interval > 3` | **1.008** peak for `entra.signins.interactive` |
| `g2o-collector-degraded-sustained` | 6h max of `scrape_success_ratio < 1` | **exactly 1**, every hour of 7 days |
| `g2o-record-integrity-loss` | `record_outcomes{outcome=~"dropped\|errored"} > 0` | records were `deduped`, a normal outcome |

None of them was close. The scrapes genuinely succeeded — the collector polled a frozen 15-minute window, re-fetched records already in `SeenIDs`, and deduped them. `graph2otel_collector_availability` reported `state=healthy, reason=success`. No error was logged because there was no error.

**The fingerprint is `fetched == mapped == deduped` with the `emitted` series entirely ABSENT.** `entra.signins.interactive` recorded fetched 2013 / mapped 2013 / deduped 2013 over 7d and no `emitted` series at all. Three Grafana detection rules were starved of input for 11 days while showing green.

## The trap in writing this rule

The obvious expression is wrong:

```promql
increase(...{outcome="emitted"}[24h]) == 0
```

`== 0` **never matches an absent series**, and absent is exactly what the `emitted` series was. A rule written that way would go green over the very incident it was built for — the same "guard asserts one layer above the bug" defect that let #417 itself sit undetected, and that #419's tests were explicitly designed against. Use `unless`:

```promql
(sum by (tenant_id, collector) (increase(graph2otel_record_outcomes_total{outcome="fetched"}[24h])) > 0)
unless
(sum by (tenant_id, collector) (increase(graph2otel_record_outcomes_total{outcome="emitted"}[24h])) > 0)
```

**Any test for this rule must be driven by a series set where `emitted` is missing, not zero.** A fixture that emits a zero-valued `emitted` series proves nothing.

## Why this ships PAUSED

A genuinely quiet window collector re-polling its overlap window and deduping every record is **indistinguishable from a livelock** by this expression alone. On a small tenant that is a normal steady state, not a fault. Enabled by default it would fire on correct behaviour, and an alert that fires on correct data trains the reader to ignore the signal — which is how the next 11-day freeze goes unnoticed.

**Unblock condition:** measure, per collector, how long the longest legitimate all-deduped run is on this tenant. Set the window above it, then enable. The measurement is the work here; the PromQL is the easy part.

## Open question worth answering first

Is `record_outcomes` even the right source? A watermark that has not advanced is the *direct* statement of this fault, and the checkpoint store already holds it. A `graph2otel.collector.watermark_age` gauge — or simply exporting the watermark timestamp — would make this a one-line staleness rule with none of the quiet-tenant ambiguity above, and would also cover the case where a collector fetches nothing at all because its window is frozen in the future. That may be a better fix than any expression over outcome counters.

Decide that before writing the rule.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decide: outcome-counter expression vs a new watermark-age signal. Record the reasoning on this issue.
- [ ] Whichever is chosen, a test driven by the REAL shape — `emitted` absent, not zero — that is watched to fail before it passes.
- [ ] Rule added, paused, with its unblock condition and the measurement needed to satisfy it stated on the rule, in the runbook and in `alerts/README.md`.
- [ ] Runbook section names the #417 fingerprint explicitly so a responder recognises it.
- [ ] `make check` green.

comments.body:
## Decision: watermark signal, not an expression over `record_outcomes`

Answering the "open question worth answering first" in the body. **The watermark wins, and the deciding fact is one the issue did not have.**

### The fact

`logpipeline.Poll` advances the watermark to `to - SafetyLag` **even when the window drained zero new records** — `internal/logpipeline/logpipeline.go:403-421`:

```go
// The watermark always advances at least to `to - SafetyLag` once this
// window has been fully drained, even when it drained zero NEW records:
// the window up to `to` has been confirmed empty (or fully deduped), so
// there is no reason to re-scan it forever.
candidate := to
if sawAny {
    candidate = newest
}
```

This collapses the whole reason the body gave for shipping paused. The body says:

> A genuinely quiet window collector re-polling its overlap window and deduping every record is **indistinguishable from a livelock** by this expression alone.

That is true of the outcome-counter expression and **false of the watermark**. A quiet collector's watermark keeps advancing at its poll interval, because an empty window is still a processed window. Only a collector whose *window* stopped moving freezes it. So the quiet-tenant ambiguity — the thing that forced the paused ship and made "measure the longest legitimate all-deduped run" the blocking work — does not exist on this signal at all. That measurement is no longer needed and is not being done.

### Two further reasons

- **It covers a case no outcome counter can see.** A watermark frozen in the *future* fetches nothing, so there are no outcomes to count and `fetched > 0 unless emitted > 0` matches nothing. `time() - watermark` reads it directly.
- **The seam already exists.** `collector.CheckpointReporter` / `CheckpointStateOf` (#178) is the read-only cursor accessor the admin status page already uses. The metric reads through it, so there is no second source of truth for durable progress and nothing new to keep in sync.

### Shape

`graph2otel.collector.watermark_timestamp` — a gauge carrying **Unix epoch seconds of the cursor itself**, not an age. The value is a fact; an age is derived against a clock, and the clock that matters is the alerting backend's, not the exporter's. `time() - metric` keeps the arithmetic visible. Same convention as Prometheus's own `process_start_time_seconds`.

Three exclusions, each of which would otherwise publish a permanently-stale series and page on a correct collector:

| skipped | why |
| --- | --- |
| blob cursors | durable progress is a byte offset; the `Watermark` field carries no meaning |
| zero watermark (cold start) | a zero `time.Time` is `Unix() == -62135596800`, i.e. **year 1, not epoch 0** — it would claim a two-millennia-old cursor on a collector that simply has not run yet |
| non-`CheckpointReporter` | every inline `SnapshotCollector`; persists no cursor |

### On the `unless` trap in the body

Still correct, and preserved — the runbook and `alerts/README.md` doc block 3 both carry it, because anyone investigating this fault will reach for `record_outcomes` and needs to know `== 0` never matches an absent series. It is documented as an investigation note rather than as the rule.

### The rule still ships paused — for a different reason

Not quiet-tenant ambiguity. The threshold. It is normalized by `graph2otel_collector_expected_interval_seconds` (same one-to-one vector match as `g2o-collector-staleness`; both metrics carry exactly `(tenant_id, collector)`), and `20` is a guess sized to clear `SafetyLag` — which is subtracted from the watermark, is per-collector, and is **not exported**, so it inflates the ratio by an unknown amount that hurts the fastest collectors most.

**Unblock condition:** observe `(time() - graph2otel_collector_watermark_timestamp_seconds) / graph2otel_collector_expected_interval_seconds` across every window collector for at least one full week on a live tenant, take the per-collector maximum, set the threshold above the largest. That measurement was impossible before this metric existed, which is why it is the unblock rather than a prerequisite.

Closed by `1e952db`. `make check` green.

**Shipped:** `graph2otel.collector.watermark_timestamp` (`internal/collector/watermark.go`), emitted per tenant on the shared self-obs report ticker; a Self-obs dashboard panel *Window watermark age (seconds behind now)*; `g2o-collector-watermark-stalled` (paused, with its unblock condition on the rule, in `docs/runbooks.md` and in `alerts/README.md` doc block 3); and a correction to doc block 3, which claimed scrape staleness covered a stalled watermark — #417 disproved that, and the wrong sentence is part of why the freeze went unnoticed.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [x] Decide outcome-counter vs watermark, reasoning recorded — see the comment above.
- [x] Test driven by the real shape, watched to fail. It was also **sabotage-checked**: reverting the skip condition publishes 3 series instead of 1, and the two bogus ones come out at `-6.21355968e+10` — which is how the year-1 detail was found. A zero `time.Time`'s `Unix()` is **not** epoch 0.
- [x] Rule added, paused, unblock condition stated on the rule, in the runbook and in `alerts/README.md`.
- [x] Runbook names the #417 fingerprint explicitly, with the measured numbers (staleness 1.008, degraded 1, availability healthy, 2013/2013/2013 outcomes with no `emitted` series).
- [x] `make check` green.

**One follow-up worth knowing about, deliberately not done here:** `SafetyLag` is not exported, which is the only reason the threshold is a guess. Exporting it (or exporting watermark age already net of it) would turn the one-week measurement into arithmetic. Not filed as an issue — the measurement is cheap and the metric now exists, so the week of observation is the faster path unless it turns out the ratios are wildly uneven across collectors.

title: Self-obs: a livelocked collector is still invisible — nothing watches the #417 fingerprint

body:
## Summary

`graph2otel_otlp_delivery_export_failures_total` is panelled ("Exporter callback rates by signal", Self-obs → OTLP delivery) and has **no alert rule**. An exporter callback failure is the process's own report that a batch it built did not reach the backend — the most general data-loss signal graph2otel has — and nothing watches it.

## Why this is the highest-value rule we do not have

It would have caught [#419](https://github.com/rknightion/graph2otel/issues/419) on the day it started. **Live-measured on m7kni 2026-08-06:**

```
sum by (signal) (increase(graph2otel_otlp_delivery_export_failures_total[2d]))
  {signal="logs"}     2.0006
  {signal="metrics"}  2.0006
```

Exactly the two HTTP 400s in #419's report. Instead, they were found by grepping container logs, and only because someone went looking.

More importantly it is **generic**. `g2o-record-attrs-truncated` guards the one backend limit we now know about. This rule catches every rejection class — a label-count limit, an auth expiry, a payload-size cap, a limit Grafana Cloud adds next year — with no requirement that we predicted it first. That is the difference between a guard and a lesson.

## Scope

One rule in `grafana/build_rules.py`:

- `g2o-otlp-delivery-failing` — `sum by (signal) (increase(graph2otel_otlp_delivery_export_failures_total[15m])) > 0`, `for: 0m`, severity `warning`, category `record-integrity`, **enabled**.

Enabled at `>0` with no baseline needed: an export failure is never a normal steady state. Grouped by `signal` (logs vs metrics) because the two fail for different reasons and a metrics-side failure is a different investigation from a logs-side one.

Deliberately **only** `export_failures`. `shutdown_failures` moves on ordinary restarts and `force_flush_failures` is a shutdown-path concern; folding them in would make the rule fire on a deploy, and an alert that fires on correct behaviour trains the reader to ignore it. Both stay panel-only.

Wired to the existing "Current exporter degradation by signal" panel, with a runbook section and an `alerts/README.md` doc block.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `g2o-otlp-delivery-failing` added and enabled, linked to the OTLP delivery panel.
- [ ] Runbook section in `docs/runbooks.md` covering the four mandatory headings, and stating that this rule is the generic backstop the per-limit rules are not.
- [ ] `alerts/README.md` doc block.
- [ ] `make check` green.
- [ ] Pushed to the m7kni stack and confirmed by content read-back.

comments.body:
Done in 71eb181 (pushed to main).

**What landed:** `g2o-otlp-delivery-failing` — enabled, `sum by (signal) (increase(graph2otel_otlp_delivery_export_failures_total[15m])) > 0`, for=0m, severity warning. Grouped by `signal` so a logs-only failure (the #419 shape) is distinguishable from a metrics-path failure.

**Why `export_failures` and not `delivery_degraded`:** degraded is a gauge that reports current state; failures is the counter that increments once per rejected export. The two HTTP 400s that motivated #419 show up as `export_failures{signal="logs"}` = 2.0006 over the 2-day window — measured, so the rule would have fired on the original incident.

**The prohibition it replaced:** `test_no_delivery_alert_is_added` (d6d960d, #268) banned any alert on `graph2otel_otlp_delivery_*`. Its stated reason, from `docs/signals.md`, is that these metrics travel through the metrics exporter and may be unobservable in the backend precisely while metrics delivery is failing. That reason supports "this cannot be the metrics-path watchdog" — it does not support "no alert at all", because a logs-path failure is fully observable via the metrics path. The gate is now `test_a_delivery_alert_states_its_self_reporting_blind_spot`: any rule referencing these metrics must carry the phrase "cannot be the metrics-path watchdog" in its description. The blind spot is documented in the rule description, `docs/runbooks.md`, and `alerts/README.md` doc block 8.

**Verification:**
- `make check` green — exit 0 read from a file, not a pipe.
- `make rules` — 18 alert rules (10 enabled, 8 paused), 0 recording rules.
- Sabotage: replacing the caveat phrase with "is fine actually" failed the new gate; reverted.
- Deployed: `make rules-push GRAFANA_CONTEXT=m7kni`, then `make rules-readback` → `compared: 18, absent: [], divergent: {}`, `g2o-otlp-delivery-failing` present in `matching`. `ungrouped` status is the known cosmetic API limitation, unchanged.

body:
## Summary

The two self-obs metrics that exist specifically to make **data loss** visible are the two nothing pages on:

- `graph2otel_event_over_horizon_total` (#401) — records dropped as older than the backend's 7-day accept window. **Record loss.**
- `graph2otel_event_attrs_truncated_total` (#419) — records whose attributes were clipped to fit Loki's 64 KiB structured-metadata limit. **Content loss.**

Both are panelled on the Self-obs board; neither has an alert rule. Meanwhile `g2o-record-integrity-loss` already fires at `>0` on `record_outcomes{dropped|errored}`, so the family precedent is "any loss is worth knowing about". A metric that only reports loss, and that nobody is watching, is the same failure mode #419 was filed for one level up.

## Scope

Two rules in `grafana/build_rules.py`, in the existing `record-integrity` category, wired to their existing panels, with runbook sections.

### `g2o-record-attrs-truncated` — ENABLED

`sum by (tenant_id, collector, ingest_transport) (increase(graph2otel_event_attrs_truncated_total[15m])) > 0`, severity `warning`.

Enabled by default because the measured rate is 2-3 records/day on m7kni (#419), so `>0` is not noisy, and because `attrs_truncated_keys` on the clipped record is currently **the only way to identify the oversized record shape** — #419's live-wire sweep cleared every reachable source, so this alert firing is the diagnostic.

### `g2o-record-over-horizon` — PAUSED

Same shape on `graph2otel_event_over_horizon_total`, severity `warning`.

Ships **paused** deliberately. Per the panel's own description and #401, a nonzero value is EXPECTED on a blob-derived stream: those replay historical records, so a record can age past 7 days by ordinary aging with nothing misconfigured. Enabled-by-default would page on normal behaviour. It belongs in the repo as an opt-in an operator turns on once their baseline is known — and the unblock condition is exactly that: know your steady-state rate, then set the threshold above it and enable.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `g2o-record-attrs-truncated` added, enabled, linked to the "Record size limit" panel.
- [ ] `g2o-record-over-horizon` added, paused, linked to the "Backend accept window" panel, with its unblock condition stated in the runbook.
- [ ] Runbook sections for both in `docs/runbooks.md` (the rule gate requires a `#<uid>` anchor).
- [ ] `make check` green.
- [ ] Rules and dashboard pushed to the m7kni stack.

body:
## Summary

The OTLP log exporter is getting per-batch HTTP 400s from the Grafana Cloud gateway because a record's structured metadata exceeds Loki's 64 KiB limit. The batch is rejected, so **those log records are lost**, and the only trace is an `otel sdk error` line.

Observed on camden, 2026-08-06 (2 occurrences in 24h):

```
level=ERROR msg="otel sdk error" error="failed to send logs to https://otlp-gateway-prod-gb-south-1.grafana.net/otlp/v1/logs:
400 Bad Request (body: stream '{service_name=\"graph2otel\"}' has structured metadata too large:
'135305' bytes, limit: '65536' bytes ...)"
```

A second occurrence reported `'74478' bytes` and `3 errors like:`, so it is per-entry, not a one-off.

## Likely source

`entra.graph_activity` records carry two very large attributes straight off the wire — a live record sampled from Loki has `roles` holding **69 comma-separated Graph scopes** (~2.3 KB on its own) plus `wids`. A record for an app with a large role set will blow the 64 KiB structured-metadata budget by itself. This wants confirming against the actual rejected records before fixing.

## Why it matters

This is silent log-record loss on the SIEM feed, and it is invisible to every existing guard: the drop happens **after** the emitter, so `graph2otel_record_outcomes_total` counts the record as `emitted`, and `graph2otel_collector_availability` stays healthy. The only signal is an SDK error line in the container log. Per CLAUDE.md the accept-window case is a loud per-entry 400 and that is the evidence of loss — same shape here, and nothing is watching for it.

## Scope to decide

Not yet diagnosed to a specific attribute. Options once confirmed:
- cap/truncate the offending attribute(s) at the emitter boundary with an explicit marker, or
- drop `roles`/`wids` from the log record and expose them another way, or
- split oversized records.

Whatever is chosen, an oversized record must not silently take its whole batch down with it, and the loss must be counted rather than only logged.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Reproduce: attempted against the live wire. NOT identified from surviving data — a rejected record is by definition absent from Loki, and every reachable source was swept and cleared (see the closing comment). `attrs.truncated_keys` on the clipped record is now the permanent identifier.
- [x] Failing test first, at the emitter boundary, over an oversized attribute set.
- [x] Oversized records no longer reject their batch; the mitigation is counted in `graph2otel_record_outcomes_total` (or an equivalent explicit metric), not only logged.
- [x] `make check` green.

comments.body:
Fixed by 864e6c6 (pushed to `main`).

## The identification did not land, and here is exactly how far it got

A rejected record is not in Loki — that is what rejected means — so the offending shape cannot be read off surviving data. I swept every source graph2otel actually reads and measured raw record sizes on the wire. **Nothing anywhere near 64 KiB survives, and the issue's prime suspect is cleared:**

| source | how measured | records | max bytes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `insights-logs-microsoftgraphactivitylogs` (the `entra.graph_activity` suspect) | blob read as `graph2otel-poller` | 3688 | **6679** |
| all 42 blob-ingest containers, 3 newest blobs each | same | ~9k | **14488** (`deviceprocessevents`) |
| `DeviceEvents.AdditionalFields` | `runHuntingQuery` KQL, 24h | 4658 | **4993** — Microsoft caps its own string columns near 5000 |
| `CloudAppEvents.RawEventData` | same, 24h | 65590 | **16160**, 0 over 30k |
| O365 Management Activity, all 5 content types | `manage.office.com` feed, 23h | 29209 | **16151** (`Audit.AzureActiveDirectory`, a chunked `additionalDetails`) |
| every `event_name` present in Loki, 24h | 100 events sampled | ~100k | **17451** (`entra.role_definition`, Global Administrator — and that one is already capped at 300 actions) |
| `serviceAnnouncement/issues` | Graph, 100 items | 100 | 38839 raw, but only ~1.1k reaches a record |

So `entra.graph_activity` is **not** the offender: its `roles` field is real but its whole record tops out at 6679 bytes on the wire. `ExposureGraphNodes` does have a 530775-byte row in the data lake (1 of 1005326), but that collector emitted **zero** records in 7d, so it is not the live source either.

Two other things worth recording: **camden has been on 6215b4f (#417 + #418) since 14:01 today**, so the 24h log window that carried the two errors is gone and the current zero-error rate is not a baseline. And the errors were ~2-3 records/day out of ~400k, so an emitted-vs-landed deficit is not detectable by counting.

**Conclusion: the offender is a rare record no reachable sample contains, which is precisely the case a generic guard handles and a targeted one does not.** The fix makes the guard itself the identifier — `attrs.truncated_keys` on the clipped record names the field, permanently, for this shape and every future one.

## The fix

`telemetry.WithAttributeBudget`, a sibling of the `#401` horizon guard, at the same seam and for the same reason: it is the one boundary every record crosses, and the only one that knows which collector produced it.

- Measures a record's attributes **exactly as Loki measures structured metadata** (sum of key + rendered value lengths), rendering through the same `logKV` the exporter uses so the two cannot drift.
- Over `MaxAttributeBytes` (60000 = 65536 less the **live-measured 627–653 bytes** of resource/scope attributes the OTLP→Loki translation folds into the same entry, plus margin), it **water-fills**: one common value ceiling across the whole set. Every attribute survives, every small one survives **intact**, and two equally huge values are clipped equally rather than one being sacrificed. A `[]string` is clipped by whole elements, a string on a rune boundary — a clipped value is never a malformed one.
- **Degraded, never dropped** — #114 applied inside a record. No attribute is dropped by name; the only content exclusion in this project is still secrets.
- Counted by `graph2otel_event_attrs_truncated_total{tenant_id, collector, ingest_transport}`, panelled on the Self-obs board ("Record size limit"), and marked on the record itself: `attrs_truncated`, `attrs_truncated_bytes`, `attrs_truncated_keys`, plus `attrs_dropped` for the pathological keys-alone-exceed-budget case.

Query for the offender once it fires:

```logql
{service_name="graph2otel"} | attrs_truncated = "true"
```

## Tests, and proof they can fail

Written first, watched fail. Two layers, because a guard asserted one layer above the bug is a recurring defect here:

- `attrbudget_internal_test.go` drives a record through a **real `sdklog` provider with a production-shaped resource** and measures what the **exporter** would ship. Sabotaged (`if true ||` at the top of `LogEvent`) it reports `exported record carries 135839 bytes of structured metadata, limit is 65536` — the exact #419 magnitude.
- `scheduler_test.go` pins the **wiring**, not just the decorator. Sabotaged (guard removed from `runEmitter`) it reports `record reaching the exporter carries 200017 bytes`.
- 13 behavioural tests over the clip itself. Sabotage failed 7 of them.

`make check` exit **0**, read from a file, not a pipe.

## Follow-up

The one thing this cannot do is tell you the offender before it next fires. Once the new image is on camden, `graph2otel_event_attrs_truncated_total` naming a collector plus `attrs_truncated_keys` naming the field closes that out — worth a look in a day or so, especially as #417's backfill may make it more frequent.

title: Log records silently lost: structured metadata exceeds Loki's 64 KiB limit, batch rejected with HTTP 400

body:
## Summary

`entra.signins.interactive` polls **v1.0** `/auditLogs/signIns` with no `signInEventTypes` filter (the v1.0 default is the interactive slice). The `signInEventTypes` property **does not exist on the v1.0 signIn resource**, so `mapSignIn` never sets the `sign_in_event_types` attribute on a polled interactive record — while all three blob-ingested sign-in streams do carry it.

Live-measured 2026-08-06 as `graph2otel-poller`:

```
v1.0  /auditLogs/signIns?$top=5&$select=id,createdDateTime,signInEventTypes  -> 400 BadRequest
beta  /auditLogs/signIns?$top=5&$select=id,createdDateTime,signInEventTypes  -> 200, 5 rows
```

Dropping `signInEventTypes` from `$select` makes v1.0 return 200. So the property is beta-only, exactly as the `FilterExtra` comment in `signins.go` already records for the *filter* — the same is true of the *projection*.

## Impact

Any consumer that identifies interactive sign-ins by `sign_in_event_types == "interactiveUser"` matches **zero** records, while the same query works for the non-interactive / service-principal / managed-identity streams. It is a silent asymmetry: one of four streams in the same event name is missing a field the other three always have, so a query written against live data from the other three looks correct and returns nothing.

This is currently masked by #417 (the interactive stream emits nothing at all). Fixing #417 alone will **not** make interactive sign-ins queryable by event type — both are needed.

## Proposed fix

`mapSignIn` derives the attribute from the wire field. For the interactive stream that field is absent, so the spec should supply it: give `spec` the event-type label it represents (`interactiveUser` for the v1.0 stream) and have the mapper fall back to it when the record carries no `signInEventTypes`. The wire value still wins when present, so the beta streams are unchanged and a future v1.0 that starts returning the property is picked up automatically.

Wire-over-docs note: the fallback must be keyed off the stream spec, not hardcoded in the mapper, because the same `mapSignIn` serves all four streams.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Failing test first: a v1.0-shaped interactive record with no `signInEventTypes` maps to `sign_in_event_types="interactiveUser"`.
- [ ] A record that *does* carry `signInEventTypes` keeps the wire value (no regression on the three beta streams).
- [ ] The fixture is a real v1.0 sign-in shape, not hand-written.
- [ ] `internal/wirecheck` declaration reviewed: the attribute is now always set for this stream.
- [ ] `make check` green.
title: sign_in_event_types is never set on v1.0-polled interactive sign-ins (beta-only property)

body:
## Summary

Eight window collectors on the m7kni tenant have been polling the **same 15-minute window from 2026-07-26** every tick for 11 days, emitting nothing. The cold-start-target completion test is unsatisfiable for any window collector with a non-zero `SafetyLag`, so once a collector enters cold-start it never leaves.

Live-measured 2026-08-06 from `checkpoints/scheduler-<tenant>.json` on camden — every stuck entry has `hwm == coldTarget - 15m` exactly:

| collector | cold-start target | hwm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `entra.signins.interactive` | 2026-07-26T14:45:54Z | 2026-07-26T14:30:54Z |
| `entra.security_alerts` | 2026-07-26T14:45:55Z | 2026-07-26T14:30:55Z |
| `entra.security_incidents` | 2026-07-26T14:45:54Z | 2026-07-26T14:30:54Z |
| `entra.agent_risk_detections` | 2026-07-26T14:45:54Z | 2026-07-26T14:30:54Z |
| `entra.service_principal_risk_detections` | 2026-07-26T14:45:56Z | 2026-07-26T14:30:56Z |
| `intune.audit_events` | 2026-07-26T14:45:56Z | 2026-07-26T14:30:56Z |
| `intune.autopilot_events` | 2026-07-26T15:00:55Z | 2026-07-26T14:45:55Z |
| `intune.enrollment_events` | 2026-07-26T14:45:54Z | 2026-07-26T14:30:54Z |

`m365.activity` and `mdca.discovery_parse` hold a zero-valued (cleared) target and are healthy, which is the control.

## Mechanism

1. `runTick` freezes `coldTarget = now - Lag` on first sight of a window collector with no checkpoint (`internal/collector/scheduler.go`).
2. While the target is set, `windowNow` is pinned to `coldTarget + Lag`, so `nextWindow` returns `to == coldTarget` on every tick.
3. `logpipeline.Poll` returns `highWater = candidate - cfg.SafetyLag` where `candidate <= to`. So `hwm <= coldTarget - SafetyLag`, **strictly before `coldTarget`** whenever `SafetyLag > 0`.
4. `runWindow` clears the target only on `!hwm.Before(coldTarget)` — unsatisfiable. The tick-level retry uses the same `!last.Before(coldTarget)` predicate, so it never fires either.
5. The target is never cleared, `windowNow` stays pinned, and the collector re-polls `[watermark-overlap, coldTarget]` forever. Every record in it is already in `SeenIDs`, so it is fetched → mapped → **deduped**, and nothing is emitted.

`DefaultSafetyLag` is 15m and no collector overrides it, so this reproduces for every logpipeline window collector that ever enters cold-start.

## Why nothing caught it

- `graph2otel_collector_availability` reports `state=healthy, reason=success` — the poll genuinely succeeds. A healthy collector that has emitted zero records for 11 days.
- `graph2otel_record_outcomes_total{collector="entra.signins.interactive"}` over 7d: `fetched 2013, mapped 2013, deduped 2013`, and the `emitted` series **does not exist**. `deduped == fetched` with no `emitted` is the fingerprint.
- No error is logged, because there is no error.

Downstream blast radius: three Grafana detection rules (`g2o-signin-anomaly`, `g2o-defender-crit`, `g2o-security-incident`) have had **zero input** for 11 days while showing green.

## Fix

The completion test must be about the **window that was polled**, not the watermark it produced. The backfill is finished when the polled window's upper bound has reached the frozen target, i.e. clear on `!to.Before(coldTarget)` in `runWindow`. The scheduler must not need to know a collector's `SafetyLag`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Failing test first: a window collector whose `CollectWindow` returns `to - SafetyLag` clears its cold-start target and advances on the next tick.
- [ ] Regression test pinning the invariant: a cold-start target is never carried for more than the ticks needed to reach it, for `SafetyLag` both zero and non-zero.
- [ ] `MaxWindow`-sliced backfill still completes (target cleared only on the final slice, not the first).
- [ ] `make check` green.
- [ ] Stuck targets cleared on camden and the eight collectors observed catching up (emitted > 0).
title: Cold-start target never clears: 8 window collectors livelocked on one 15-minute window for 11 days

body:
## Symptom

`grafana-sync` has failed on **every run since 2026-07-29**. The `publish dashboard to
GitSync` job succeeds each time; `publish alert rules` fails.

| head | result | commit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a6b0038` | failure | fix(selfobs): declined 403 no longer ratchets staleness (#408) |
| `7b04434` | failure | fix(alerts): 10m pending window on g2o-collector-staleness |
| `4fce107` | failure | feat(entra): GSA per-connection traffic logs |
| `e627e02` | failure | feat(entra): related-tenant governance posture |
| `7ef1aa6` | success | ci(grafana): publish the dashboard and alert rules to the m7kni stack |

Consequence: the m7kni stack has been silently diverging from this repository for six
days while the workflow reported the drift but could not correct it.

## What the run reports

```json
"push": {"phases": {"create": {"pushed": 0, "failures": []},
                    "group":  {"pushed": 0, "failures": []}},
         "pushed": 0, "failures": [], "ungrouped": []},
"created": ["g2o-collector-degraded-sustained"]
```

`pushed: 0` alongside a `created` list naming a rule it demonstrably *did* create — the
read-back in the same run found that rule present and content-matching. The counters are
fiction. The read-back then reports `12 divergent`, every one of them only
`__panelId__` / `dashboard_path`: source `447/445/467/466`, live `437/435/457/456`. The
dashboard panel ids moved, the rules regenerated against them, and the updates never landed.

## Root cause — gcx output mode, live-verified

`gcx` emits JSON only in **agent mode**, auto-detected from `CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_CODE`,
`CURSOR_AGENT`, `GITHUB_COPILOT`, `AMAZON_Q` or `GCX_AGENT_MODE`. Verified 2026-08-04 by
unsetting all six and re-running a gcx command: it printed a human table, not JSON.

None of those are set on a GitHub Actions runner. `_push_dir`
(`grafana/rules_deploy.py:172-186`) scans stdout for a `{`-prefixed `gcx.mutation_batch`
document; against text output it finds none and falls through to its initialisers,
returning `{"pushed": 0, "failures": []}` **unconditionally**.

The asymmetry is visible at the call sites — the two reads were fixed for this and the
write was missed:

```
rules_deploy.py:280   resources get    … "-o", "json"   ✓
rules_deploy.py:393   resources get    … "-o", "json"   ✓
rules_deploy.py:172   resources push   … (no -o)        ✗
```

The workflow's own folder-resolve step carries a comment about the gcx banner appearing
"in AGENT mode only", so the mode difference was known and fixed there.

## Why this is worse than a wrong counter

`failures: []` is the damaging half. Phase 2 pushes every rule **with** its group labels;
the rules on the stack are ungrouped, so those pushes are refused with
`cannot set group when updating un-grouped rule`. Phase 3 exists precisely to retry those
with the group labels stripped — its own comment records that leaving it out *was a live
bug, not a theoretical gap*, because a rejected push applies nothing: annotations, query,
thresholds and all.

With `failures: []` the `UNGROUPABLE` branch never fires, phase 3 never runs, and the
identical live bug is back by a different route. The read-back is the only reason it is
visible at all — it is doing its job.

## Why the existing tests could not catch it

Every gcx fake in `grafana/tests/test_rules_deploy.py` returns a JSON `gcx.mutation_batch`
string, including the two tests written specifically about the UNGROUPABLE retry. They
assert on the layer *above* the bug: given parseable input the parser works, and the
failure mode is that the input is not parseable. A test cannot catch a defect it feeds
around.

## Scope

1. **Pass an explicit output flag on the push** — `-o json` on `resources push`,
   matching the two `resources get` calls. (`scripts/grafana-prune-rules.py`'s delete
   needs nothing: it discards stdout and guards on the return code, so it is
   mode-independent by construction. An earlier draft of this issue called it a latent
   instance — that was WRONG, asserted from the missing flag without reading the call.) Explicit flag rather than setting `GCX_AGENT_MODE` in the
   workflow: the env-var list is gcx's, not ours, and the two reads already establish the
   in-repo convention.
2. **Make "parsed nothing" an error, not a zero.** `_push_dir` must raise when it finds no
   `gcx.mutation_batch` document. A push whose result could not be read is an unknown
   outcome, and reporting an unknown outcome as `0 pushed, 0 failures` is what turned a
   flag omission into six days of silent drift. This is the fix that generalises.
3. **Test at the right layer** — a gcx fake returning *text* output, asserting the raise.

## Explicitly NOT doing: deleting the rules to fix their grouping

Considered and rejected on the repo's own recorded evidence. The API cannot place a rule in
a named group at creation (`cannot set group when creating a new rule`) and cannot group it
afterwards (`cannot set group when updating un-grouped rule`) — both measured, both recorded
in `docs/deploying-observability.md` under "One known limitation". `RuleSequence` is not a
way round it: it requires at least one recording rule and this repo ships none (#297).

So delete-then-recreate lands every rule ungrouped again — the same state, minus an alerting
window while they do not exist. Grouping stays cosmetic and stays hand-fixable in the UI;
the read-back already reports those rules as `matched_content_ungrouped`, a clean pass. Once
this issue is fixed the *content* is correct, which is the part that decides whether an alert
fires.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `push()` raises when gcx returns unparseable (text-mode) output, pinned by a test
      whose fake returns the real human one-liner rather than JSON.
- [ ] `resources push` passes `-o json`, pinned by a test.
- [ ] `make check` green.
- [ ] `grafana-sync` goes green on the commit that fixes it, and `make rules-readback`
      reports `matched` or `matched_content_ungrouped` — not `drifted`.
- [ ] The 12 stale `__panelId__`/`dashboard_path` annotations are corrected on the live
      stack, and `g2o-collector-degraded-sustained` (#408) is present and enabled.

comments.body:
**Correction to the issue body.** The claim that `scripts/grafana-prune-rules.py:147` carries a latent instance of this bug was WRONG — I asserted it from the missing `-o json` without reading the call. Its `gcx()` helper returns stdout unparsed and the delete call discards it entirely, guarding on the return code instead (gcx exit 4 = partial failure raises `PruneError`). It is mode-independent by construction. No change made there, and none needed.

The rest of the diagnosis held up under the fix.

**Green, and verified live.** `grafana-sync` succeeded on `912fca0` — the first success since 2026-07-29.

Two commits, because the guard caught the first fix:

- `fc5cb94` — `-o json` on the push, and `_push_dir` raises on an unread result instead of reporting zero.
- `912fca0` — the raise then caught that fix's own parser against real CI output. `-o json` **pretty-prints one document**; agent mode emits compact JSON-lines. A line-at-a-time scan reads nothing from a pretty-printed document (first line is a bare `{`), so the run failed again — but loudly, and with the true push result in the diagnostic: `succeeded: 0, failed: 15`, every failure `cannot set group when updating un-grouped rule`. Exactly the state that had been invisible for six days. `_mutation_batch` now tries whole-document first, line-at-a-time second.

**The successful run's receipt:**

```
phases.group.pushed:   0   (all 15 refused — UNGROUPABLE, as expected)
phases.regroup.pushed: 15  (phase 3 fired and every rule's content landed)
readback: compared 15, divergent {}, status matched_content_ungrouped
```

Phase 3 running at all is the proof: it is reached only via the failure list that #413 was emptying.

**Live read-back of the two rules this touched:**

| uid | for | paused | `__panelId__` | severity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `g2o-collector-staleness` | `10m0s` | false | 436 | critical |
| `g2o-collector-degraded-sustained` | `30m0s` | false | 434 | warning |

The staleness rule read `5m` and panel `426` live before this — the alert notification that started the investigation carries `viewPanel=426` in its `dashboard_path`, which is the stale annotation in the wild. Both are now current, and #408's new warning rule is deployed and enabled.

**On deleting the rules to fix their grouping:** not done, and it would not have worked. The receipt above confirms the recorded API limitation — all 15 rules sit outside the named group because the API cannot group a rule at creation and cannot group it afterwards. A delete-and-recreate lands them ungrouped again, minus an alerting window. `matched_content_ungrouped` is a clean pass and the content — the part that decides whether an alert fires — is correct.

Incidentally verified the agent-mode banner half of the fix: the live read-back above was produced by calling `rules_deploy.gcx(parse=True)` from a Claude Code session, which is the exact path that used to raise `returned invalid JSON`.

title: fix(ci): grafana-sync silently pushes nothing — gcx emits JSON only in agent mode, so every push reports 0/0

body:
## Symptom

`g2o-collector-staleness` (severity: critical) has been paging continuously on tenant
`4b8c18bd-2f9f-4227-af55-9f1061cf9c32` for three collectors:

| collector | interval | ratio at time of writing | first went stale (UTC) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `entra.risky_agents` | 900s | 14.0 | 2026-07-31 15:00 |
| `entra.agent_risk_detections` | 1800s | 7.0 | 2026-07-31 18:00 |
| `purview.retention_labels` | 3600s | 3.0 | 2026-07-30 17:00 |

Before those timestamps all three sat at staleness 0. The ratios reset only because the
container restarted 2026-08-04 ~14:10 UTC; prior to that they had ratcheted past **53 hours**.

## Root cause, part 1 — tenant-side, permanent, not our bug

camden container logs (`live-measured 2026-08-04`):

```
entra.risky_agents           GET /beta/identityProtection/riskyAgents
                             → 403 {"code":"Forbidden","message":"Your tenant is not licensed for this feature."}
entra.agent_risk_detections  GET /beta/identityProtection/agentRiskDetections
                             → 403 (identical body)
purview.retention_labels     GET /v1.0/security/labels/retentionLabels
                             → 500 {"ErrorCode":"DataInsightsRequestError",
                                    "Message":"DataInsights command(GET) FAILED - Forbidden."}
                             GET /v1.0/security/triggerTypes/retentionEventTypes → same
```

These are well-formed Graph JSON 403s naming licensing, not scope denials — no app-role grant
will clear them (`denial-layer-before-scope`). The agent-risk pair losing entitlement within
three hours of each other on Jul 31 reads as the Entra agent-risk preview being withdrawn from
the tenant; the Purview failure is a separate event a day earlier with a different shape
(Purview DataInsights backend refusing, surfaced as a Graph 500).

## Root cause, part 2 — the actual defect

Two of the three collectors already **decide** this is a tolerable steady state and say so:

- `internal/collectors/entra/riskyagents/riskyagents.go:150-159` — logs at INFO
  ("skipping risky agents … feature not enabled on this tenant") and **returns nil**. Its
  doc comment states outright: *"A 403 is a graceful info-skip … not a failure."*
- `internal/collectors/purview/retentionlabels/retentionlabels.go:281` — same shape.

But both call `outcomes.Cause(recordoutcome.CausePermissionDenied)` first, and
`internal/collector/scheduler.go:280` computes:

```go
healthy := outcome.Result == recordoutcome.ResultEmpty ||
    outcome.Result == recordoutcome.ResultSuccess
```

A cause-carrying outcome summarizes to `ResultFailure` (`recordoutcome.go:277-292`), so
`healthy` is false, so `scheduler.go:313` never advances `lastSuccess`. Staleness therefore
climbs without bound and the **critical** staleness alert pages forever over a condition the
collector explicitly classified as fine and that no operator action can clear.

Confirmed on the wire: `graph2otel_scrape_outcomes_total{collector="entra.risky_agents"}` has
**only** a `result="failure"` series — there is no success series at all.

So the graceful skip is graceful in the log and in the return value, and a hard failure in
every metric that matters. `entra.agent_risk_detections` is worse: it has no skip path at all
(`internal/collectors/entra/agentriskdetections/`), so the window collector hard-fails with a
returned error on every poll.

## Scope

Three changes, deliberately kept separable.

1. **Stop `permission_denied` ratcheting staleness** (`internal/collector/scheduler.go`). A run
   that completed — no panic, no returned error — whose only cause is `permission_denied` is a
   correctly-handled permanent refusal, not a scrape that failed to happen. It should stamp
   `lastSuccess`. Everything else stays exactly as it is: the WARN "degraded outcome" log, the
   `result="failure"` outcome metric, `graph2otel.scrape.success` = 0, `scrape.errors`,
   collector availability, the status page. Only the staleness ratchet changes.

   Deliberately **not** doing: a new `CauseNotEntitled`. `CausePermissionDenied` is set at 30+
   call sites and is part of the status contract's priority order
   (`recordoutcome.go:310-320`, consumed by #292); threading a new cause through all of them
   buys nothing the `runErr == nil` test does not already give.

2. **Give `entra.agent_risk_detections` the 403 skip its sibling has.** Same 403, same tenant,
   same meaning — one collector treats it as an info-skip and the other as a hard error. Port
   the `isForbidden` path from `riskyagents.go`.

3. **Add a warning-severity degradation alert** (`alerts/rules/`, via `grafana/build_rules.py`).
   Change (1) removes the only thing that currently surfaces a genuinely revoked scope, and
   `g2o-detect-graph-403-burst` does not cover it (it is paused, needs blob-sourced
   `entra.graph_activity`, and watches tenant-wide caller behaviour rather than our own health).
   Replacement: sustained `graph2otel_scrape_success_ratio == 0` over a multi-hour window at
   **warning**, not critical — a lost grant is worth knowing about and is not worth a page.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Scheduler test: a collector that returns nil with `Cause(CausePermissionDenied)` and zero
      records does **not** grow `graph2otel.scrape.staleness` across consecutive runs, while
      still reporting `scrape.success` = 0 and `scrape_outcomes_total{result="failure"}`.
- [ ] Scheduler test (the guard that matters): a collector that returns a **non-nil error**
      carrying `permission_denied` DOES still ratchet staleness — the exemption is for the
      completed-and-declined path only, not for "any 403 anywhere".
- [ ] `entra.agent_risk_detections` returns nil and records `permission_denied` on a 403,
      pinned by a test against a verbatim live 403 body.
- [ ] New warning alert rule generated by `make rules`, with the drift gate green.
- [ ] `make check` green.
- [ ] Deployed to camden and verified live: the three collectors' staleness stops climbing and
      `g2o-collector-staleness` resolves, while their outcome metrics still read as degraded.

## Non-goals

- Restoring the tenant's agent-risk entitlement or the Purview DataInsights permission. Both
  are tenant-side and outside this repo. Note for the record: the two `entra` collectors are
  `Experimental` (beta surface) and are expected to come back if/when the preview returns.
- Reviewing the ~30 other `CausePermissionDenied` sites. Several are sub-fetch 403s inside
  otherwise-successful collectors, which summarize to `ResultPartial` and are *also* unhealthy
  and *also* ratchet staleness. That is the same class of bug at a different blast radius, but
  none of them are firing on m7kni today and folding them in would make this change unreviewable.

comments.body:
Landed in `a6b0038` (pushed to main; issue auto-closed by the closing keyword).

**What shipped**

- `internal/collector/scheduler.go` — new `declinedPermission()`; a run that completed with no returned error, no panic, and `cause=permission_denied` now stamps `lastSuccess`. Nothing else softened: `scrape.success` stays 0, the outcome stays `result=failure`, availability/status still show degraded, the WARN line still fires every tick.
- `internal/collectors/entra/agentriskdetections/` — gained the 403 decline its sibling `entra.risky_agents` already had. Watermark left untouched on a decline, so it resumes from the same point if the entitlement returns.
- `alerts/rules/g2o-collector-degraded-sustained.yaml` (new, **warning**, enabled) — `max_over_time(graph2otel_scrape_success_ratio[6h]) < 1`, `for: 30m`. Covers the revoked-consent-grant case that the staleness rule used to catch by accident.
- Runbook section + `alerts/README.md` doc block 3 updated to state what staleness no longer covers and why.

**Tests** — the narrow-exemption guard is the one that matters: `TestScheduler_ErroredPermissionStillRatchetsStaleness` pins that a 403 the collector could *not* handle still goes stale. Without it, "any 403 anywhere" would silence the staleness alert entirely.

**Incidental, already-drifted things fixed in passing:** the staleness runbook and `alerts/README.md` both still said `for: 5m` after `7b04434` moved it to 10m. Note the *live* rule on grafana.m7kni.com also still reads 5m — `make rules-push` has not been run since that commit, so the stack is behind the repo on that rule independently of this change.

**Remaining acceptance criterion:** deploy to camden and confirm the three collectors' staleness stops climbing while their outcome metrics still read degraded. Waiting on the `:main` image build.

title: fix(selfobs): a correctly-handled tenant-entitlement 403 still ratchets scrape staleness, paging critical forever

body:
The rule is `noDataState: Alerting` on purpose - "the whole query returning zero rows means every collector's self-obs signal went dark at once". That is correct, but it also means the rule cannot tell "the exporter died" from "the network between a healthy exporter and Grafana went away". On the reference deployment those are the same wire: the site firewall is the route out, and rebooting it takes 10-15 minutes.

Measured on the 2026-08-01 17:09-17:25 reboot (boot at 17:15, ~7 min of downtime). The rule is `severity: critical` with no `domain`, so it reaches IRM through the notification policy's `severity=critical` route, and every IRM route posts to its MS Teams channel the instant an alert group is created - the escalation chain's 15-minute wait step delays the personal page but not the channel post. So the pending window is the only lever.

`for: 5m` at a 5m evaluation interval is one extra evaluation, which is not enough margin for anything. 10m is two, and still well inside the 3x-expected-interval tolerance the threshold itself is built around.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `for` is 10m in the `g2o-collector-staleness` entry in `grafana/build_rules.py`
- [ ] The description text no longer says "for 5m"
- [ ] `make rules` regenerated, `alerts/rules/g2o-collector-staleness.yaml` committed
- [ ] Verified live at `for=10m` after deploy

## Note

Already patched live on 2026-08-01 via the classic provisioning rule-group API as immediate relief. Two traps hit on the way, worth recording: the rule carries `grafana.app/managedBy: classic-api-provisioning`, so `gcx resources push` 409s on it (`cannot update with provided provenance 'api', needs 'api'`), and the single-rule provisioning PUT 400s on a zero interval because this repo's push gives every rule its own asterisk-padded pseudo-group. The working path is GET/PUT on `/api/v1/provisioning/folder/<uid>/rule-groups/<url-encoded padded group name>`. Without this change the next deploy reverts it.

comments.body:
Live value is `10m0s` (verified by pulling the rule back), so the acceptance criteria are met in the stack. But the deploy path itself is **broken and was already broken before this change** - flagging it here rather than silently leaving a green issue over a red pipeline.

`grafana-sync` has failed on every run since 7ef1aa60 (last success 2026-07-29T20:23Z; failures at e627e02d and 4fce107f the same evening, both before this work). `make rules-push` aborts with `"status": "drifted"` because the live rules carry **stale panel ids** against the generated ones - `g2o-collector-staleness` is `__panelId__` 426 live vs 436 generated, `g2o-mdca-parse-failing` 297 live vs 307, and the drift report lists 13 rules ungrouped. A dashboard panel renumbering landed in the generator and never reached the stack.

Consequences for this issue:

- The 10m in `grafana/build_rules.py` will not deploy until that drift is cleared. It is committed and correct; it is just not what put 10m in the stack.
- Nothing will revert the live 10m either, for the same reason - the pusher refuses to write at all while drifted.
- Once the panel-id drift is resolved and a sync succeeds, the generator and the stack agree at 10m and this is self-consistent again.

The panel-id drift needs its own issue - it is unrelated to alert timing and predates it.

title: g2o-collector-staleness: 10m pending window so a firewall reboot doesn't page

body:
## What

Automate publication of this repo's generated Grafana artifacts to the m7kni stack on push to `main`. Part of a three-repo effort — see `rknightion/opnsense-exporter#529` for the shared design.

| artifact | path |
|---|---|
| `dashboards/graph2otel.json` | commit into `rknightion/gc-gitsync-m7kni` as `graph2otel/graph2otel.json` |
| `alerts/rules/*.yaml` | `make rules-push` — **this repo's own deployer**, not a bare `gcx resources push` |

## The dashboard had never been deployed

`dashboards/graph2otel.json` was generated, gated and committed, but **no dashboard by that UID or title existed on the stack**. `docs/deploying-observability.md` documents a manual `gcx dashboards create -f`, which had evidently never been run against m7kni. It now ships through GitSync like the other two repos' dashboards.

It lands in its **own** GitSync folder, `graph2otel/` → Grafana folder **"graph2otel Dashboards"** (UID `graph2otel-dashboards`), deliberately distinct from the existing **"graph2otel"** *alerts* folder (`frb4qp`) the rules job writes. Two folders, two purposes, no title collision. Landed as `gc-gitsync-m7kni@0695878`.

## Rules keep using this repo's own deployer

`make rules-push` is retained rather than replaced with `gcx resources push`, because the committed manifests carry `grafana.app/folder: REPLACE_WITH_FOLDER_UID` and an unresolved token fails with 403 rather than filing the rule somewhere wrong. It also needs `grafana.com/provenance: api` + `--omit-manager-fields`, which is the **opposite** of what the other two repos need (see #529) — do not unify them.

The workflow therefore also runs `make rules-readback` after the push: a push that reports success is not a deployment that matches source.

## Two CI-specific wrinkles

1. **`rules_deploy.py` pins the gcx context by NAME and refuses to run without one**, so env-var auth alone is not enough. The workflow writes a throwaway `$GCX_CONFIG` file (umask 077, removed in an `if: always()` step) defining a `m7kni` context.
2. **The alerts folder UID is resolved at run time from its title**, since a folder UID is stack-specific and this is a public repo. gcx prepends a `{"class":"hint",...}` banner **in agent mode only**, so it is filtered by content rather than dropped by position — a bare `tail -n +2` eats the only line of real output on a CI runner.

## Scope

- [x] `.github/workflows/grafana-sync.yml` — push to `main` path-filtered on `dashboards/**`, `alerts/**`, `grafana/**`, plus `workflow_dispatch`
- [x] `scripts/grafana-prune-rules.py` — the deployer is create-or-update only, so a rule dropped from the generator would keep evaluating forever. The expected set comes from `rules_deploy.project_all(include_detections=False)` — the deployer's own notion, not a filename heuristic — so the paused portable detection pack stays excluded exactly as `make rules-push` excludes it.

## Verified live before merge

- `make rules-push` + `make rules-readback` with the service-account credential: status `matched_content_ungrouped`, **exit 0** (the expected state — the API cannot group a rule it created)
- Prune dry-run: 14 live vs 14 in repo, **0 orphans**
- Dashboard reconciled by GitSync, reporting `managedBy=repo src=graph2otel/graph2otel.json`

## Acceptance

- [x] Dashboard deployed and GitSync-managed for the first time
- [x] Rules push and read-back verified end-to-end with the CI credential
- [x] Prune verified dry-run and excludes the detection pack

comments.body:
Shipped in `7ef1aa6`. First workflow run on the real push: [green](https://github.com/rknightion/graph2otel/actions/runs/30488234472).

Run confirmed every CI-specific part of the design in one go: `resolved graph2otel -> frb4qp` (title to UID at run time), `this repository deploys 14 rules` (detection pack correctly excluded), `live=14 repo=14 orphans=0`, and `rules-readback` exiting 0 on `matched_content_ungrouped`.
