body:
## What & why

graph2otel reports on a tenant's configuration and identity activity, but nothing about whether the Microsoft-side services those signals depend on are actually healthy. When sign-in volume drops or Intune check-ins stall, the first triage question is "is this us or is this Microsoft?" — and today that question can only be answered by a human opening the admin portal, outside the alerting path.

Microsoft publishes service health as a first-class Graph surface. Polling it puts service status on the same dashboard and in the same alert rules as the rest of the tenant's telemetry, so a sign-in anomaly can be correlated against a live Exchange incident instead of investigated cold. It is also about the cheapest signal we can add: two small collections, no paging pressure, no per-entity fan-out.

## API surface

| Endpoint | Version | App permission | Paging | Filter/delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /admin/serviceAnnouncement/healthOverviews` | v1.0 | `ServiceHealth.Read.All` | 100/page | none |
| `GET /admin/serviceAnnouncement/issues` | v1.0 | `ServiceHealth.Read.All` | 100/page, `Prefer: odata.maxpagesize` up to 1000 | none |
| `GET /admin/serviceAnnouncement/messages` (optional, see below) | v1.0 | `ServiceMessage.Read.All` | 100/page | none |

`healthOverviews` supports `?$expand=issues`, which folds both reads into one request. Worth measuring — if it holds, prefer it.

Docs:
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/serviceannouncement-list-healthoverviews?view=graph-rest-1.0
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/serviceannouncement-list-issues?view=graph-rest-1.0

`serviceHealthIssue` carries `id`, `title`, `classification` (Incident/Advisory), `status`, `service`, `feature`, `origin`, `isResolved`, `startDateTime`, `endDateTime`, `lastModifiedDateTime`, `impactDescription`, `posts`.

## Telemetry model

Both shapes, from the same fetch.

**Metrics — bounded, tenant-shaped:**

- `m365.service_health.services.total{status}` (gauge) — count of services in each health status. Bounded by the status enum (~7 values). This is the alertable one: `> 0` on a degraded status fires regardless of which service broke.
- `m365.service_health.status{service}` (gauge) — numeric status enum per service. Bounded by the M365 service count (tens). Document the enum mapping in `docs/signals.md`; do not invent a companion mapping metric to carry it.
- `m365.service_health.issues.total{classification, status}` (gauge) — open issue count by Incident/Advisory and status. Bounded.

**Log twin — `m365.service_health_issue`, one log per issue:**

Issue `id`, `title`, `impactDescription`, `service`, `feature`, `classification`, `status`, `isResolved`, `startDateTime`, `endDateTime`. These are per-entity and unbounded over time — an issue id or title as a metric label would produce a series with exactly one sample, which is the pathological TSDB case and buys nothing a LogQL `count by` over the twin cannot answer. Per the cardinality rule they are log attributes, and they must not be dropped: the title and impact description are the whole operational value.

Severity: map `classification` and `isResolved` onto the log severity scale (an unresolved Incident outranks a resolved Advisory).

Message center posts (`/admin/serviceAnnouncement/messages`) are a coherent part of the same surface but answer a different question — upcoming change announcements rather than current health — and need a second scope (`ServiceMessage.Read.All`). Build them as a separate collector under the same package, default-off, or split to a follow-up if this issue gets long. Do not fold them into the health collector's scope declaration.

## Constraints & gotchas

- No delta query and no time filter on either collection, so these are snapshot reads, not `WindowCollector`s. The issue log twin therefore re-emits open issues every cycle — that is correct for a snapshot twin, but pick an interval (15m is a reasonable start) that keeps the log volume sane.
- `endDateTime` is null for unresolved issues; do not compute a duration from it unguarded.
- Both collections are small. Do not add paging cleverness that the data does not justify.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Add collector `internal/collectors/m365/servicehealth` implementing `SnapshotCollector`, registered under the `m365.servicehealth` collector key.
- [ ] Emit `m365.service_health.services.total{status}` and `m365.service_health.status{service}` from `/admin/serviceAnnouncement/healthOverviews`.
- [ ] Emit `m365.service_health.issues.total{classification, status}` from `/admin/serviceAnnouncement/issues`.
- [ ] Emit one `m365.service_health_issue` log per issue carrying id/title/impactDescription/service/timestamps, with severity derived from classification + isResolved.
- [ ] Declare exactly `ServiceHealth.Read.All`; no broader scope.
- [ ] Test with a faked Graph client + `Recorder`: metrics carry no per-issue attribute (id/title/timestamps), and every issue in the fixture produces exactly one log.
- [ ] Test that a null `endDateTime` on an unresolved issue does not panic or emit a bogus duration.
- [ ] Document the `m365.service_health.status` enum mapping and the stream selector caveat in `docs/signals.md`.
- [ ] Live-verify against a real tenant; record the observed status values.
- [ ] `make check` green.

comments.body: Route decision to make first (added 2026-07-17, #146; flagged originally on #100): service health is exposed by **two** transports this app can already speak — Graph `/admin/serviceAnnouncement/*` (`ServiceHealth.Read.All`) **and** the O365 Management API's `ServiceHealth.Read` role (client already built: `internal/o365activityclient`; the role is already app-only-capable on this tenant). Pick deliberately, not by accident of which client the implementer reaches for. Graph route is the default assumption in the body; if the Management API route wins, record why here.

## Decision (maintainer, 2026-07-18): Graph `/admin/serviceAnnouncement/*`

Transport chosen: **Graph `/admin/serviceAnnouncement/*`** (`ServiceHealth.Read.All`), not the O365 Management API route.

Rationale: it's the modern, richer resource model (health overviews + the incident/advisory message stream), v1.0, and native to the raw-REST collector framework — chosen by fit, not by the convenience of the o365activityclient already existing for #100. Client reuse alone was never a good reason to take the thinner legacy surface.

Build note (wire-over-docs): verify `/admin/serviceAnnouncement/healthOverviews`, `/issues`, and `/messages` live as `graph2otel-poller` before writing mappers, and pin fixtures to those captures — Microsoft's docs have been wrong on this project's load-bearing details before.

## Blocked on a scope grant — `ServiceHealth.Read.All` is not consented to graph2otel-poller

Ran the wire-first check the build note asks for (probe live as `graph2otel-poller`, cert on camden, `graph.microsoft.com/.default`, 2026-07-18 ~14:38Z). All three endpoints 403 with the empty-message shape Graph returns for a missing app permission:

| endpoint | result |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /admin/serviceAnnouncement/healthOverviews` | **403** |
| `GET /admin/serviceAnnouncement/healthOverviews?$expand=issues` | **403** |
| `GET /admin/serviceAnnouncement/issues` | **403** |
| `GET /admin/serviceAnnouncement/messages` | **403** |

Confirmed it's a grant gap, not a transient error: decoded the access token's `roles` claim (the definitive list of consented app permissions). It carries neither **`ServiceHealth.Read.All`** nor **`ServiceMessage.Read.All`**. The poller does hold the adjacent security scopes (`SecurityAlert.Read.All`, `SecurityIncident.Read.All`, `ThreatHunting.Read.All`, `IdentityRisk*`) but not the service-announcement pair.

### What this blocks

The CLAUDE.md rule is wire-over-docs — mappers pinned to live captures, never written from Microsoft's docs — and this issue's own build note says verify the three collections live *before* writing mappers. With a 403 I can capture nothing, so the build is parked here, not started blind.

### Unblock condition (tenant mutation, needs maintainer approval)

Grant + admin-consent **`ServiceHealth.Read.All`** (Application) to the `graph2otel-poller` app registration. That alone covers `healthOverviews` + `issues` (the two required collections in the AC). The optional message-center collector additionally needs **`ServiceMessage.Read.All`** — defer that with the messages collector itself unless you want it in the same grant.

Once consented I'll re-probe, pin fixtures to the captures, record the observed `status`/`classification` enum values here, and build. Nothing else about the issue changes — transport and telemetry model stay as decided.

`[live-measured 2026-07-18, #119]`

## Unblocked — `ServiceHealth.Read.All` granted; wire verified; building

Maintainer authorized the grant (2026-07-18). Performed it via `az` as `rob@m7kni.io` (GA): a single `appRoleAssignment` POST to the poller SP both assigns and admin-consents the application permission — assignment id `NhU3E1...`, `ServiceHealth.Read.All` (`<guid-51>`) → `graph2otel-poller`.

Re-probed as `graph2otel-poller` (fresh token) — the 403s are gone:

| endpoint | result |
| --- | --- |
| `/admin/serviceAnnouncement/healthOverviews` | **200** — 29 services |
| `/admin/serviceAnnouncement/healthOverviews?$expand=issues` | **200** — expand holds (17/29 carry issues) |
| `/admin/serviceAnnouncement/issues` | **200** — 100/page, `@odata.nextLink` present |
| `/admin/serviceAnnouncement/messages` | **403** — `ServiceMessage.Read.All` still ungranted (the optional message-center collector; deferred, as the body allows) |

### Wire facts (live-measured 2026-07-18, #119) — mappers pinned to these

- **`healthOverviews`** record is minimal: `{ "service", "status", "id" }`. Observed `status` values this snapshot: `serviceOperational`, `serviceDegradation` (Exchange, M365 suite, Defender XDR, Intune, SharePoint degraded). The full `microsoftServiceHealthStatus` enum is wider; the numeric mapping metric will document all documented values, not just the two live now.
- **`issues`** carries the full field set: `id, title, classification (advisory|incident), status (serviceRestored, serviceDegradation, investigationSuspended, postIncidentReviewPublished, …), service, feature, featureGroup, origin, isResolved, startDateTime, endDateTime, lastModifiedDateTime, impactDescription, posts[]`.
- **`endDateTime` is null on unresolved issues — confirmed live** (`isResolved:false` rows have `endDateTime:null`). The duration-guard AC is real, not hypothetical.
- `$expand=issues` works, folding both reads into one request — will use it.

Building the collector now: `internal/collectors/m365/servicehealth`, `SnapshotCollector`, scope exactly `ServiceHealth.Read.All`, metrics + one `m365.service_health_issue` log twin per issue.

## Shipped — `c581d13`, `make check` green

`internal/collectors/m365/servicehealth`, `SnapshotCollector`, exactly `ServiceHealth.Read.All`. Emits the three bounded gauges + the `m365.service_health_issue` twin from one `?$expand=issues` fetch. Status-enum ladder documented in `docs/signals.md` (no companion mapping metric). Tests cover: no per-issue metric label, unresolved-only twinning + dedup, **null `endDateTime` on an unresolved issue doesn't panic or emit a bogus value**, the unmapped-status → -1 fallback, and the all-healthy (zero-issue) path.

### Live-verified (2026-07-18, graph2otel-poller, post-grant)

Observed on m7kni, recorded per the AC:
- **Service statuses:** `serviceOperational`, `serviceDegradation` (degraded at probe time: Exchange Online, M365 suite, Defender XDR, Intune, SharePoint Online).
- **Issue classifications:** `advisory`, `incident`. **Issue statuses:** `serviceRestored`, `serviceDegradation`, `investigationSuspended`, `postIncidentReviewPublished`. **isResolved:** both true and false present; **`endDateTime` null on unresolved — confirmed**.
- 29 services, 232 issues via expand, **6 unresolved**. The wire field set matches the collector's structs exactly (service/status/id + the 12 issue fields).

### One deliberate deviation from the AC — flagging for veto

The AC says "every issue in the fixture produces exactly one log." I scoped the **twin to UNRESOLVED issues only**. Rationale: the API returns the tenant's whole retained issue history (226 of 232 long-resolved), and this snapshot collector re-emits every cycle — twinning all of them re-ships hundreds of months-old resolved incidents every 15m for no operational gain. The body's own wording ("re-emits **open** issues every cycle") points the same way, and the aggregate `issues.total{classification,status}` gauge still covers resolved ones. If you'd rather twin every issue, it's a one-line change (drop the `if !is.IsResolved` guard) — say the word and I'll flip it.

Message-center posts (`/messages`, `ServiceMessage.Read.All`) remain a separate deferred collector as the body allows — that scope is still ungranted (the probe 403s on `/messages`), so it's not in scope here.

Closed by `c581d13`.

Maintainer confirmed (2026-07-18): keep the **unresolved-only** twin as shipped — good. No change; recording the endorsement so the deviation is settled, not just proposed. The message-center half (`ServiceMessage.Read.All` + `/admin/serviceAnnouncement/messages`) is being built as a separate default-off collector under the same package, tracked in a follow-up issue.

body:
Split out of #117, whose deployment half (checkpoint persistence + fail-fast on an unwritable dir) landed in `aad052d`. This is the remaining half: the async-job lifecycle and the configurable backfill window.

## 1. In-flight async job ids are not persisted, so a restart orphans and re-creates

The checkpoint schema (`internal/checkpoint/checkpoint.go:24-43`) is exactly:

`Schema`, `TenantID`, `Endpoint`, `Watermark`, `OverlapWindow`, `SeenIDs`

**No in-flight job/query id.** Both async engines create a server-side job then poll it:

- `internal/jobpipeline` — `POST /security/auditLog/queries` → poll status → page records (`m365.unified_audit`)
- `internal/exportjob` — `POST /deviceManagement/reports/exportJobs` → poll status → download CSV (the Intune export-report collectors)

A restart between create and completion abandons the job; the next tick creates a **new** one for the same window. Nothing lists existing jobs to adopt an orphan.

**Not theoretical.** Live-verified 2026-07-16 (#100): an audit-log query took **over 10 minutes** to reach `succeeded`. `m365.unified_audit` polls every 30 min, so roughly a third of its cycle has a job in flight — a wide window for a redeploy to land in. And these are the worst APIs to duplicate against: #98 found rapid audit-query creation returns **429**, and CLAUDE.md records the Intune reports-export API at **48/min per app**.

**Severity: wasted calls, orphaned server-side jobs, and throttle pressure — NOT data loss.** The watermark correctly does not advance on failure (`scheduler.go:310-316`), so the window is simply retried. Worth fixing, but it does not lose events; do not inflate it.

## 2. The backfill window is not configurable

`InitialLookback`, `MaxWindow`, `Overlap` and `SafetyLag` are per-collector **consts** today, not config keys. Maintainer requirement: **backfill must be configurable**, at least for logs (metrics can stay near-realtime — a snapshot collector re-derives state every tick, so a missed metric tick costs nothing).

`InitialLookback` is the one that matters most: it bounds how much history a cold start recovers, and therefore how long an outage can be before events are silently lost. That loss path is real and survives `aad052d` — persistence stops *routine* loss, but a genuinely fresh checkpoint (new tenant, wiped volume, first deploy) still only reaches back `InitialLookback`.

## What is NOT broken — verified, do not re-investigate

- **The `MaxWindow` clamp is correct.** `internal/collector/window.go:25-26` sets `to = from.Add(maxWindow)`, anchored to the **old watermark**, not to `now`. A long outage walks forward in `MaxWindow`-sized chunks over successive ticks and catches up **losslessly** — as `window.go:11-12` documents and `logpipeline/scale_test.go:101-102` asserts. An earlier hypothesis that this silently skipped the gap was **wrong**.
- **Emit-then-checkpoint ordering is correct** (`scheduler.go:308-324`): `CollectWindow` runs first; on error the checkpoint is not advanced and the next tick retries the same window ("at-least-once, no gaps").
- **Checkpoint writes are atomic** (`store.go:103-108`): `.tmp` + `os.Rename`, pinned by a test that a stray `.tmp` cannot corrupt state (`store_test.go:115`). A kill mid-write cannot corrupt the checkpoint.

The engine is sound. Resist rewriting it.

## Fix sketch

- Add an optional in-flight job field to the checkpoint (id + created-at + the window it covers). It is a **persisted on-disk format** with a `Schema` version field (`checkpoint.go:24`) — use it; an older binary must tolerate the new field and vice versa.
- On start, if a job id is present **and its window matches the window this tick would request**, resume polling it instead of creating a new job. If the window has moved on, discard it.
- **Expire stale in-flight jobs** after a bounded age so a dead job cannot wedge a collector forever.
- Expose `InitialLookback` (at minimum) as config. Any new key must satisfy #103's config registry + drift-check gate (`G2O_` prefix, `__` nesting, `docs/env-vars.md` regenerated via `scripts/regen-generated.sh`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In-flight job id persisted and **adopted** on restart by both `jobpipeline` and `exportjob`
- [ ] A test proves a restart mid-job **resumes** rather than creating a second job
- [ ] Stale in-flight jobs expire rather than wedging the collector
- [ ] Schema migration via the existing `Schema` field; forward/backward tolerance tested
- [ ] Backfill window configurable (at minimum `InitialLookback`), registered per #103's drift gate
- [ ] Live-verified: restart camden mid-cycle while an audit query is in flight; confirm no second query is created
- [ ] `make check` green

comments.body:
## Constraint for the backfill-window half: Loki caps the *useful* window, not the checkpoint

Surfaced on #89 while choosing a blob-retention period. Maintainer:

> *"as loki cant backfill more than 13 days anyway I'm happy with 7d"*

This bounds acceptance criterion **"Backfill window configurable (at minimum `InitialLookback`)"** in a way the issue body does not currently account for.

**The point:** Loki rejects samples older than its `reject_old_samples_max_age`. graph2otel emits logs over OTLP into Loki. So an `InitialLookback` wider than that age is **not a longer recovery — it is guaranteed silent rejection at the backend.** graph2otel would page the Graph endpoint, map the records, ship them, and have Loki drop them on ingest. The operator sees Graph calls being made, no errors from the collector, and no logs in Grafana.

That is a worse failure than a short lookback, because it *looks* like it is working.

**Implication for this issue:** `InitialLookback` should not be a free-form duration. When the key lands, it needs at minimum a **validation warning** when set beyond the backend's accept window — a config registry entry (#103) that documents the ceiling rather than an unbounded duration string. The exact ceiling is backend-specific (Grafana Cloud's limit is the one that matters here; the maintainer puts it at ~13 days), so this is likely a documented warning threshold rather than a hard clamp — graph2otel should not pretend to know every backend's retention policy.

**Do NOT read this as "backfill doesn't matter".** The requirement stands: an outage must not silently lose events, and `aad052d` only fixed the *routine* case. The correction is narrower — the useful recovery window has a **downstream ceiling**, so the config key should guide operators to it instead of letting them set 30d and wonder where the logs went.

Cross-ref: #89's storage transport uses a **7-day blob lifecycle** for exactly this reason, so the fallback-ingest path is already aligned with the ceiling.

## Shipped `4ab4523` - one acceptance criterion is NOT met, see the bottom

`make check` green.

### In-flight job adoption

The checkpoint gains an optional job record (id, created-at, and the window it covers) behind the existing `Schema` field. A job is adopted only when its window matches the window this tick would request, and discarded otherwise; stale jobs expire after a bounded age so a dead job cannot wedge a collector forever. Forward and backward schema tolerance are both tested - an older binary tolerates the new field and vice versa.

### Configurable backfill

`backfill.initial_lookback` / `G2O_BACKFILL__INITIAL_LOOKBACK`, registered per #103's drift gate with `docs/env-vars.md` regenerated.

Default `0` means each collector keeps its own built-in lookback, so behaviour is unchanged. **Zero collector files were touched**: the override lands at the `RegisterWindow` call site in the composition root rather than being plumbed through nine collectors.

Set beyond ~13 days it **warns rather than clamps**, per this issue's comment. A wider lookback is not a longer recovery, it is silent rejection at Loki - which looks like it is working, and is a worse failure than a short lookback. But graph2otel must not pretend to know every backend's retention policy, so it is a documented warning threshold. Warnings are non-fatal via `cfg.Warnings()`; `Validate()` stays error-only.

### Left alone deliberately

The `MaxWindow` clamp, emit-then-checkpoint ordering, and atomic checkpoint writes were re-read and confirmed correct, exactly as this issue's "What is NOT broken" section says. The engine is sound.

### 🔴 Outstanding: the live verification

This acceptance criterion is **not** met:

> - [ ] Live-verified: restart camden mid-cycle while an audit query is in flight; confirm no second query is created

GitHub auto-closed this on the commit keyword. The code is tested and green, but **the behaviour this issue exists to fix has not been observed on the real tenant** - and this repo's own history is emphatic that unit tests do not substitute for that (#109: three collectors passed unit tests and failed every cycle live). Reopen if this should stay open until camden confirms it.

## The outstanding live-verify: runnable procedure

The one unmet acceptance criterion from `4ab4523`. Recording it here so it survives, and so whoever runs it is not re-deriving it.

Every value below was **re-derived from the shipped code and checked**, not quoted from memory.

### Target: `m365.unified_audit`

The only realistic one. From `internal/collectors/m365/unifiedaudit/unifiedaudit.go`:

```
createPath      = "/security/auditLog/queries"
checkpointKey   = createPath + "#m365"   -> "/security/auditLog/queries#m365"
interval        = 30 * time.Minute
lag             = 1 * time.Hour
safetyLag       = 1 * time.Hour
initialLookback = 4 * time.Hour
maxWindow       = 24 * time.Hour
```

A 30-minute interval against a query that took **over 10 minutes** live (#100) means roughly a third of the cycle has a job in flight. That is the window to land a restart in. The export collectors run every 6h and finish in minutes, so timing a restart into one by hand is impractical; that path is covered by `TestExport_RestartAdoptsInFlightJob` through the real file store instead.

It is `Experimental`, so it needs an explicit opt-in:

```yaml
collectors:
  m365.unified_audit:
    enabled: true
```

### 1. Find the checkpoint dir

```bash
systemctl cat graph2otel 2>/dev/null | grep -i checkpoint     # systemd
docker inspect graph2otel 2>/dev/null | grep -i CHECKPOINT    # docker
CKPT=/var/lib/graph2otel/checkpoints   # <- set to whatever the above reports
ls -la "$CKPT"/*auditLog*
```

**The filename is confirmed empirically** (by running the real `checkpoint.Store`, not by reading the sanitizer):

```
TENANT-GUID___security_auditLog_queries_m365__8dab3090834ca4ff.json
```

`store.go:172` builds it as `sanitize(tenantID)__sanitize(endpoint)__<sha256[:8]>`, so `/` and `#` both become `_`. Glob on `*auditLog*`.

### 2. Watch for a query id landing before the poll finishes

```bash
watch -n10 'jq .in_flight '"$CKPT"'/*auditLog*.json'
```

`null` most of the time. In flight:

```json
{ "id": "<guid>", "created_at": "...", "window_from": "...", "window_to": "..." }
```

Note the `id`.

### 3. Restart while `in_flight` is non-null

```bash
systemctl restart graph2otel      # or: docker compose restart graph2otel
```

### 4. Verdict

```bash
journalctl -u graph2otel -f | grep -iE 'unified_audit|auditLog|429'
jq .in_flight "$CKPT"/*auditLog*.json
```

- **PASS** - the id from step 2 is unchanged after the restart, gets polled, and clears to `null` once drained. No second query, no 429.
- **FAIL** - `in_flight.id` becomes a *different* guid (the orphan-and-recreate bug this issue exists to fix), or a 429 appears from rapid create.

The restart triggers an immediate tick, which is exactly why adoption matters: without it, that tick POSTs a second query against an API that 429s on rapid create.

### Bonus: the backfill half, no timing required

```bash
G2O_BACKFILL__INITIAL_LOOKBACK=30d graph2otel -config <path>
```

Expect **one** `config advisory` line (`main.go:90`, `logger.Warn("config advisory", "detail", w)`) naming `backfill.initial_lookback`, Loki, and `reject_old_samples_max_age` - and the process must **start normally and still use 30d**. If it refuses to start, or silently clamps to 13d, that is a bug: this issue's comment is explicit that it warns, never clamps.

### Why this is still worth running

The gate covers the engine logic through the real file store in both directions. It does not cover a real Graph query, a real SIGTERM, or a real restart, which is exactly where an in-flight-job assumption breaks. #109 is this repo's own precedent: three collectors passed unit tests and failed every cycle on the live tenant.

## Live-verified on camden — the last AC is now satisfied

Restarted camden mid-cycle with an audit query in flight. **No second query was created; the in-flight query was adopted.**

Sequence (all times UTC, tenant `4b8c18bd`, `m365.unified_audit`):

```
22:04:20  restart -> tick creates query, persists in_flight immediately
22:04:22  in_flight: {"id":"<guid-52>",
                      "created_at":"2026-07-16T22:04:21.966290703Z",
                      "window_from":"2026-07-16T15:51:52.778028589Z",
                      "window_to":"2026-07-16T21:04:21.733074933Z"}
          ... still in flight 3 min later (matches #100's >10 min observation)
22:08:39  restart WHILE in flight  (in_flight still carries 889f346b)
22:08:43  in_flight cleared
          watermark: 19:51:52.778028589Z -> 20:04:21.733074933Z
```

### Why this proves adoption rather than a re-create

The watermark landed on **`20:04:21.733074933`** = the adopted job's `window_to` (`21:04:21.733074933`) minus `safetyLag` (1h), **to the nanosecond**.

A newly-created query could not produce that value. `to` is `now-lag` (`collector/window.go`), so a tick at 22:08:39 would have computed `window_to ≈ 21:08:39` and advanced the watermark to `≈20:08:39`. The observed watermark instead carries the nanosecond fingerprint of a `to` computed 4 minutes earlier, by the process that has since been killed. A fresh wall-clock read cannot reproduce it.

Ruled out the one alternative explanation: a `MaxWindow` clamp would make `to` deterministic (`from + maxWindow`) and therefore reproducible across restarts, which would break the fingerprint argument. It did not apply — `maxWindow` is 24h and the window span was `5h12m28.955046344s`, well under it, so `to` was purely wall-clock derived.

This also exercised the `emitAndAdvance(..., windowTo, ...)` path as documented: the watermark advanced only as far as the **adopted job's own window**, not this tick's `to`, so the remaining `21:04:21 -> 21:08:39` sliver is left for the next tick rather than skipped.

`in_flight` clearing alone would NOT have been proof — a failed/cancelled query clears it too (`jobpipeline.go:299-303`). The watermark advance is what discriminates.

- [x] Live-verified: restart camden mid-cycle while an audit query is in flight; confirm no second query is created

### Follow-up: a cold checkpoint cannot adopt (filed separately)

Found while verifying, NOT covered by the above. `CoversWindow` requires `j.WindowFrom.Equal(from)`, and on a cold checkpoint (`hasLast == false`) `nextWindow` derives `from = to.Add(-initialLookback)` where `to = now-lag` — so `from` moves with wall-clock and can never equal a persisted `WindowFrom`. A restart mid-job against a cold checkpoint therefore discards the job and creates a second one: the exact behaviour this issue removed, in the case where it is most likely (first deploy, operator restarting to tweak config).

Narrow and self-healing — once the first tick sets a watermark, `from = last` is stable and adoption works, which is why the verification above passed. Severity is unchanged from this issue's framing: wasted calls, an orphaned server-side job, and throttle pressure against an API that 429s on rapid creates (#98). Not data loss.

title: fix(checkpoint): resume in-flight async jobs across restarts + make the backfill window configurable

body:
## Summary

**The checkpoint engine is correct. The shipped deployments throw its state away.**

`docker-compose.yml` mounts **no checkpoint volume at all**, and the Helm chart defaults the checkpoint volume to **`emptyDir`**. So on the two ways graph2otel actually ships, the watermark + SeenIDs do not survive the events they exist to survive — and camden, which tracks the `:main` edge image, discards them on **every redeploy**.

Separately, neither async-job engine persists its **in-flight job id**, so a restart mid-job orphans the server-side job and creates a new one — on APIs that throttle hard.

## What is NOT broken (checked first, and my initial hypothesis was wrong)

I expected the `MaxWindow` clamp to be the data-loss path — clamp the window to 24h, advance the watermark to the clamped end, silently skip the gap. **That is not what it does, and the design is right.**

`internal/collector/window.go:25-26`:

```go
if maxWindow > 0 && to.Sub(from) > maxWindow {
    to = from.Add(maxWindow)
}
```

`to` is anchored to `from` (the **old watermark**), not to `now`. A long outage therefore walks forward in `MaxWindow`-sized chunks over successive ticks and **catches up without loss** — exactly as `window.go:11-12` documents and `logpipeline/scale_test.go:101-102` asserts. No bug. Good design.

Also verified sound:

- **Emit-then-checkpoint ordering** (`internal/collector/scheduler.go:308-324`): `CollectWindow` runs first; on error the checkpoint is **not** advanced and the next tick retries the same window — the code comment calls it "at-least-once, no gaps". Correct.
- **Atomic checkpoint writes** (`internal/checkpoint/store.go:103-108`): `.tmp` + `os.Rename`, with a test pinning that a stray `.tmp` cannot corrupt state (`store_test.go:115`). A kill mid-write cannot corrupt the checkpoint.

So the engine is fine. The bugs are at the deployment boundary and in the async-job lifecycle.

## Bug 1 — docker-compose persists no checkpoints at all (highest impact)

`docker-compose.yml:44-46` mounts only the config:

```yaml
volumes:
  - ./config.yaml:/etc/graph2otel/config.yaml:ro
```

`config.example.yaml:120` defaults `checkpoint_dir: "./checkpoints"` — a **relative path**, so it lands in the container's writable layer. That layer is destroyed when the container is **recreated**, which is precisely what `docker compose pull && up -d` does. Camden runs this way and redeploys regularly.

The example config even warns *"mount a writable, persistent path in a container"* — the docs know; the compose file does not do it.

**Consequence on every redeploy:**

- Watermark lost → each window collector restarts from its `InitialLookback` (4h for `m365.unified_audit`, 1h for `intune.audit_events`, etc.)
- SeenIDs lost → **the dedupe set is empty, so the whole re-fetched lookback window is re-emitted as duplicate log records**
- If downtime exceeds `InitialLookback` → **permanent gap**: the window between `watermark` and `now - InitialLookback` is never queried by anyone

Duplicates on every redeploy is the routine case. Gaps need a long outage, but they are silent when they happen.

## Bug 2 — Helm defaults to emptyDir

`charts/graph2otel/templates/deployment.yaml:95` → `emptyDir: {}`, with `persistentVolumeClaim` (`:92`) only when `persistence.enabled=true`. `values.yaml:47-48` describes emptyDir as the default that "already works".

`emptyDir` survives a container restart **within a pod**, but not pod deletion, rescheduling, eviction, or node drain. So the default Helm install has the same failure as Bug 1, just on a different trigger — and "works" in values.yaml means "is writable", not "persists".

## Bug 3 — no in-flight job id is persisted

The checkpoint schema (`internal/checkpoint/checkpoint.go:24-43`) is exactly:

`Schema`, `TenantID`, `Endpoint`, `Watermark`, `OverlapWindow`, `SeenIDs`

**No in-flight job/query id.** Both async engines create a server-side job then poll it:

- `internal/jobpipeline` — `POST /security/auditLog/queries` → poll → page records (`m365.unified_audit`)
- `internal/exportjob` — `POST /deviceManagement/reports/exportJobs` → poll → download CSV (the Intune export collectors)

A restart between create and completion abandons the job and the next tick creates a **new** one for the same window. Nothing lists existing jobs to adopt an orphan.

**This is not theoretical.** Live-verified 2026-07-16 (#100): an audit-log query took **over 10 minutes** to reach `succeeded`. `m365.unified_audit` polls every 30 min, so roughly a third of its cycle is spent with a job in flight — a wide window for a redeploy to land in. And these are the worst APIs to duplicate against: #98 found rapid audit-query creation returns **429**, and CLAUDE.md records the Intune reports-export API at **48/min per app**.

Severity is "wasted calls + orphaned jobs + throttle pressure", **not** data loss — the watermark correctly does not advance on failure (`scheduler.go:310-316`).

## Fix sketch

1. **`docker-compose.yml`**: add a named volume for the checkpoint dir, and set `checkpoint_dir` to an absolute path inside it. Highest value, smallest change.
2. **Helm**: either default `persistence.enabled=true`, or make the emptyDir default **loud** — values.yaml must say plainly that the default loses checkpoints on reschedule, causing duplicate logs and possible gaps. Silently defaulting to data loss is the wrong trade for a security-posture exporter.
3. **Checkpoint schema**: add an optional in-flight job field (id + created-at + the window it covers). It is a **persisted on-disk format** with a `Schema` version field (`checkpoint.go:24`) — use it; an older binary must tolerate the new field and vice versa. On start, if a job id is present and its window matches the current one, **resume polling it** instead of creating a new job; expire it after a bounded age so a genuinely dead job cannot wedge the collector forever.
4. **Config surface for backfill**: `InitialLookback`/`MaxWindow`/`Overlap`/`SafetyLag` are per-collector consts today, not config keys. The maintainer wants a **configurable backfill window**; exposing `InitialLookback` is the one that matters most, since it bounds how much history a cold start recovers. Any new key must satisfy #103's config registry + drift-check gate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `docker-compose.yml` persists the checkpoint dir across `pull && up -d` — verified by redeploying camden and confirming the watermark survives
- [ ] Helm either persists by default, or documents the emptyDir data-loss trade-off unmissably in `values.yaml`
- [ ] In-flight job id persisted and **adopted** on restart by both `jobpipeline` and `exportjob`; a restart mid-job must not create a second job
- [ ] Stale in-flight jobs expire rather than wedging the collector
- [ ] Checkpoint schema migration handled via the existing `Schema` field; forward/backward tolerance tested
- [ ] Backfill window configurable (at minimum `InitialLookback`), registered per #103's drift gate
- [ ] A test proves a restart mid-job resumes rather than recreates
- [ ] Live-verified on camden: redeploy mid-cycle, confirm no duplicate log burst and no gap
- [ ] `make check` green

## Notes

- The engine design is good; resist rewriting it. This is a deployment-wiring bug plus one missing checkpoint field.
- **Metrics are unaffected and out of scope** — snapshot collectors re-derive state every tick, so a lost checkpoint costs a metrics collector nothing. This is a logs problem.

comments.body:
## Correction: camden is NOT affected — I got that wrong

The body claims camden discards checkpoints on every `pull && up -d`. **That is false, and I should not have asserted it without checking the box.** Verified just now:

```
$ ls -land /opt/graph2otel/checkpoints
drwxr-xr-x 2 65532 65532 4096 Jul 16 11:57 /opt/graph2otel/checkpoints
$ ls /opt/graph2otel/checkpoints | head
4b8c18bd-...___auditLogs_directoryAudits__9856dfa4a51b5245.json
4b8c18bd-...___auditLogs_provisioning__2f07ead58223a523.json
...
$ docker logs --since 30m <graph2otel> | grep -c "checkpoint persist failed"
0
```

Camden's `compose.yaml` already does the right thing, and was fixed by hand:

```yaml
user: "65532:65532"
read_only: true
volumes:
  - ./checkpoints:/var/lib/graph2otel
```

paired with `checkpoint_dir: /var/lib/graph2otel` in its `config.yaml`, and the host dir chowned to `65532:65532`. Zero persist failures in 30 minutes — it works.

## What this actually changes: the bug is worse, not better

The real defect is that **the reference `docker-compose.yml` in this repo does not do what camden does.** Anyone following it gets a broken deployment; camden is fine only because it was hand-fixed and diverged from the reference.

And the reference is worse than "loses state on recreate". It sets:

```yaml
user: "65532:65532"
read_only: true
volumes:
  - ./config.yaml:/etc/graph2otel/config.yaml:ro   # <- the ONLY mount
```

with `config.example.yaml:120` defaulting `checkpoint_dir: "./checkpoints"` — a **relative** path. With `read_only: true` there is **no writable location at that path at all**, so checkpoint writes do not merely get discarded on recreate, they **fail on every single tick from the very first one**. `scheduler.go:319-325` catches that and logs a Warn + emits a self-obs metric, so it degrades quietly rather than crashing: every window collector silently re-polls its `InitialLookback` window forever and re-emits duplicate logs on every cycle, in perpetuity.

So: **camden — fine. The shipped reference — never persisted a checkpoint in its life.**

## Revised scope

Bug 1 is now "make the reference match camden's proven-working pattern", plus the permissions trap that pattern hides:

- `./checkpoints` bind mount → `/var/lib/graph2otel`, `checkpoint_dir` set to match
- **Permissions must be tolerated** (maintainer's explicit ask). This is the sharp edge: with `user: 65532` + `read_only: true`, a `./checkpoints` dir that Docker auto-creates on first `up` is **root-owned**, so the container cannot write it — and today that failure is a per-tick Warn nobody reads. Needs both the documented `chown 65532:65532` step AND a **startup check that fails fast with an actionable message** instead of degrading silently for months.

Bugs 2 (Helm emptyDir) and 3 (no in-flight job id) stand as written.

Deployment half done in `aad052d` (pushed). Remaining async-job scope split out to https://github.com/rknightion/graph2otel/issues/118 — closing this.

## What landed

- **compose reference now matches camden's proven pattern**: `./checkpoints:/var/lib/graph2otel` bind mount + `G2O_CHECKPOINT_DIR=/var/lib/graph2otel`, with the `chown 65532:65532` step documented in the header and *why* it matters.
- **`Store.Verify()` fails fast at startup** on an unwritable checkpoint dir, instead of degrading into a per-tick Warn nobody reads. Called once in `main` before tenants start (the dir is global, and `startTenants` deliberately never fails the process for one tenant). It probes with a real write-then-remove rather than inspecting mode bits, because the failure modes that matter — root-owned bind mount under `user: 65532`, read-only rootfs, full volume — aren't all visible in the bits.
- **config.example.yaml + docs/env-vars.md** state the consequence plainly; the #103 drift gate caught the doc desync on the first `make check`, which is exactly what it is for.
- **Helm**: no behaviour change — the chart was already honest about its emptyDir default, and a zero-config `helm install` cannot assume a StorageClass. Corrected one over-reassuring sentence: emptyDir cold-start re-runs the lookback "rather than silently dropping data" only holds while downtime is *shorter* than that lookback.

**Verified end-to-end, not just by unit test:** an unwritable dir aborts with an error naming the path and the chown; a writable one is auto-created and starts clean with no probe file left behind.

## Correction carried forward

This issue originally claimed camden discards checkpoints on every redeploy. **That was false** — camden was hand-fixed long ago (bind mount + `checkpoint_dir: /var/lib/graph2otel`, host dir owned `65532:65532`, zero persist failures in 30 min). The real defect was that the shipped reference had **diverged from the thing that works**, and was worse than described: with `read_only: true` and a *relative* default it could never write a checkpoint at all, from the very first tick.

Closes #117

title: fix: checkpoints are discarded on every redeploy (no compose volume, Helm defaults to emptyDir) + async job ids are not resumable

body:
## Mission

Decide whether graph2otel should adopt a **real cache layer** (Redis sidecar or similar) for Graph response data, in-flight async job state, and checkpoints — or whether in-process + a persistent volume is genuinely sufficient. Pre-v1 epic; **spike first, build only if the spike justifies it.**

Maintainer framing (2026-07-16):

> *"if our solution would benefit from a redis cache sidecar or similar for this type of data as well as our general cache that another issue mentions then we might want to explore that. Given some entra/intune/defender tenants can be huge caching 'properly' might be a worthwhile tradeoff but will let you spike that"*

## Start sceptical: what problem does the cache actually solve?

**Do not start from "Redis". Start from the measurement.** A cache only pays when the same data is fetched more than once, or when something must survive a process boundary. Establish which — if either — is true before designing anything.

The honest prior, from what we already know:

- **The one identified duplicate read is already fixed, in-process.** #87 audited every collector and concluded *"no response caching exists anywhere"*, and that the single clean win was `/deviceManagement/managedDevices` being fully paged by two collectors each cycle. That shipped as `internal/collectors/devicefleet.go` — an in-process shared fetch with a union `$select`. Its own doc is candid that it is **API etiquette, not a throttling fix**. So the known duplicate-read problem is solved without any external cache.
- **Checkpoints are already durable** via the file-based `internal/checkpoint` store (assuming the volume is actually mounted — being verified in the restart/backfill spike; if it is NOT mounted, that is the bug, and a persistent volume fixes it for free where Redis would not).
- **graph2otel is deliberately single-instance.** CLAUDE.md: *"Single-instance, no HA/leader-election in v1 — none of the polled Graph endpoints support consumer-group/delta semantics that would make multi-replica coordination pay for itself. Revisit only if a real multi-replica requirement shows up."* **Redis's main structural advantage is sharing state between processes.** If there is only ever one process, that advantage is worth nothing, and Redis is a dependency, a failure mode, and an ops burden bought for free.
- **On a huge tenant the bottleneck is probably not cache locality — it is Graph itself:** per-workload throttle ceilings, page-walk wall-clock, and the per-endpoint quirks already in CLAUDE.md (no `$count` on `managedDevices`; `$select=keyCredentials` throttled ~150/min; IPC at 1 req/s per tenant). **A cache does not reduce the first fetch, and the first fetch is the expensive one.** Verify or refute this — it is the crux of the whole epic.

If the spike concludes "a persistent volume plus the existing in-process sharing is sufficient", **that is a successful outcome**, not a failure. Say so and close.

## Phase 1 — the spike

1. **Measure before designing.** On the live m7kni tenant (and modelled up to a 10k–50k user/device tenant): where does cycle wall-clock and Graph call volume actually go? Which endpoints are paged more than once per cycle, by whom? Is there *any* repeated identical read left after `devicefleet.go`?
2. **Enumerate the candidate cacheable state**, and for each say what it would buy and whether an external store is required:
   - Graph response bodies (which endpoints repeat? what TTL is even safe given these are posture signals?)
   - Reference/lookup data that changes rarely — e.g. `consent`'s `roleNames` map, service-principal resolution, `roleDefinition` expansions. These are re-resolved per cycle and are genuinely slow-moving.
   - **In-flight async job ids** (see the linked spike) — `jobpipeline` create-query and `exportjob` create-export. This needs to survive a restart, but **that is the checkpoint store's job**, not a cache's. Do not let "cache" absorb a durability requirement that belongs in `internal/checkpoint`.
   - Checkpoints themselves — only if multi-replica ever becomes real.
3. **In-process vs external — argue it explicitly.** What does an external store give that a `sync.Map` + TTL and a mounted volume do not, *for a single-instance deployment*? If the answer is "nothing until multi-replica", the epic's real question becomes an HA question, and HA is deliberately out of v1.
4. **Cost/benefit honestly.** A Redis sidecar means: another container in compose and the Helm chart, another config surface (#103's registry + drift gate applies to every new key), another failure mode (what does graph2otel do when Redis is down — fail, or degrade to direct fetch?), another thing to secure, and cache-invalidation bugs which are their own genre. Weigh that against the measured win from step 1.
5. **Staleness is a correctness question, not just perf.** This is a security-posture exporter. A cached "device is compliant" that is 10 minutes stale is a *wrong answer* to a question someone may be alerting on. State the TTL policy per candidate and which signals must never be cached.

## Phase 2 — build (only if Phase 1 justifies it)

- Behind a clean interface so the backend is swappable and **absent by default** — a deployment with no cache must behave exactly as today.
- Config-gated per #103's registry + drift-check gate.
- Never cache anything whose staleness would make an alert wrong.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Phase 1 written up as a comment: the measurement, the candidate list, in-process-vs-external argument, cost/benefit, and a **single recommendation**
- [ ] The "huge tenants need caching" premise explicitly tested against the measurement, not assumed
- [ ] Explicit finding on whether ANY repeated identical read survives `devicefleet.go`
- [ ] Explicit statement that in-flight job durability belongs to `internal/checkpoint`, not the cache (or a reasoned argument for why it should not)
- [ ] A decision: build, or close as unjustified with the reasoning recorded so it is not re-litigated
- [ ] If built: off by default, config-gated, degrades gracefully when the backend is unavailable, TTL policy documented per cached signal
- [ ] `make check` green

## Related

- **#87** (closed) — the polling-interval/response-caching/rate-limit-headroom audit; concluded no caching existed and shipped `devicefleet.go` as the one clean win. **Read its analysis in full before re-deriving any of it.**
- The async-job-resume + restart-backfill spike — overlaps on in-flight job durability and checkpoint persistence. Sequence after it, since its findings may remove a chunk of this epic's motivation.
- CLAUDE.md's single-instance/no-HA decision is the load-bearing constraint on the "why external?" question.

comments.body: Sequencing gate lifted (2026-07-17, #146): the body says to run this after the async-job-resume/restart-backfill work — that was #117/#118, both now closed (`aad052d`, `4ab4523`), and the checkpoint volume is verified mounted+durable on camden. This spike is actionable now. As the body predicted, #117/#118 removed much of the original motivation; "in-process + a volume is enough" remains a successful outcome.

## Decision (maintainer, 2026-07-18): no Redis sidecar — but explore a local on-disk cache

**Redis/external cache: declined.** graph2otel is single-instance, so Redis's structural advantage (sharing state across processes) is worth nothing here; checkpoints are already durable on the persistent volume, the one known duplicate read (`/deviceManagement/managedDevices`) is already fixed in-process, and a cache does not reduce the *first* fetch — the expensive one. Adding a sidecar would pay ongoing dependency/ops cost for a benefit this architecture can't realize. Per this issue's own framing, "in-process + a volume is enough" is a successful outcome.

**New live question this issue now owns:** whether a **local on-disk cache file** (not an external service) would benefit the project — e.g. reduce Graph API load across restarts, reduce in-process/CPU load, or persist derived state that's expensive to recompute. This is a different question from the Redis spike and worth a small scoped investigation:
- [ ] Which reads/derived-state are expensive enough to be worth persisting locally, and which are cheap to refetch?
- [ ] Would an on-disk cache survive restarts usefully, or does the poll cadence make it moot (data stale by next poll)?
- [ ] Interaction with the existing CheckpointStore (also file-based, per-tenant) — extend it, or a separate cache?
- [ ] Net effect on API load vs added complexity, measured not assumed.

The Redis question is closed; this issue continues as the local-disk-cache exploration.

## Spike concluded: no local on-disk data cache — "in-process + a volume is enough" holds (measured)

Investigated against the code, not assumed. Answering the four checklist items, then the recommendation.

### 1. Which reads/derived-state are expensive enough to persist locally vs cheap to refetch?

**No derived/computed state is expensive.** Every collector is JSON-decode → bucket-count into bounded gauges/histograms + per-entity log twins. There is no sorting of large sets, no bulk hashing, no hot-path regex — nothing whose *result* is worth persisting to skip a recompute. So a cache could only ever save **fetch I/O, never CPU**.

The expensive *fetches* don't clear the "cacheable without going stale" bar:
- **`intune.malware` per-device sweep** — up to ~3,000 `GET .../managedDevices/{id}/windowsProtectionState` every 30m (capped at `windowsFleetSweepThreshold=3000`). This is per-device **current** protection state — the whole point is that it's fresh each poll. Caching it serves stale posture, the opposite of what a security feed wants.
- **Device fleet page-walk** (`/deviceManagement/managedDevices`) — already cached **in-process** for a 30m TTL by the #87 `CachingFleetFetcher`, shared across `intune.devices` + `intune.malware`. Lost on restart (memory only). For a 10k fleet that's ~10 pages; on m7kni (~11 devices) it's one page.
- **Async export jobs** (`intune.app_install_report` / `defender_report` / `cert_inventory_report`, 6h) — expensive (create→poll→download→parse CSV) but already **restart-covered** by #118 job adoption (below).

### 2. Would an on-disk cache survive restarts usefully, or does poll cadence make it moot?

**Largely moot.** The poll model wants current state every interval; a cache older than the interval is stale-as-current — a correctness hazard on a posture feed, not a win. Crucially there is **no server-side change signal**: grep confirms zero use of `@odata.deltaLink`, delta queries, ETags, or `If-None-Match` anywhere (the log endpoints have no delta at all — that's why every `WindowCollector` owns a watermark). So a data cache could only be **TTL-based**; it can't *know* upstream is unchanged, so it can't safely lengthen freshness beyond the poll interval. The only cross-restart reuse window is "a restart lands inside the fleet's already-accepted 30m TTL" — narrow, and restarts are infrequent.

### 3. Interaction with the existing CheckpointStore — extend it, or separate?

**Neither is attractive.** `internal/checkpoint` is purpose-built for **resume cursors**, not data: it stores a window watermark + overlap + a *bounded, evicted* seen-id set, or a per-blob byte offset, or an in-flight async-job id — one pretty-printed JSON file per `(tenant, endpoint)` key, atomic-rename write (no fsync), no size bound, with the seen-id set actively pruned to the overlap window. Storing bulk fetched data there would fight every one of those design choices (the eviction would drop it, the pretty-JSON + per-endpoint files don't suit blobs, there's no size ceiling). A data cache, if ever built, would have to be a **separate** store — but see the recommendation.

### 4. Net effect on API load vs added complexity (measured)

**API load a persistent cache could remove:** one `/subscribedSkus` call per tenant per restart (license detection is computed once at startup, ~1 small call, then a pure in-memory GUID lookup) + the fleet page-walk on a restart that lands inside the TTL. Both **small and bounded**. The genuinely high-call-count work (the ~3,000-call malware sweep, hourly fleet, 6h jobs) is either current-state-must-be-fresh or already restart-covered.

**What #117/#118 already avoid on restart** (so a cache would NOT be adding this): re-running an in-flight async export/audit job (job adoption via `Checkpoint.InFlight` + `JobRecord` scope-fingerprint), re-emitting blob bytes (per-blob byte offsets), and re-polling processed log windows (watermark + overlap + seen-ids). What a restart still re-does: the fleet page-walk (in-memory cache only) + the one license call + the next tick's normal fetches.

**Complexity a data cache would add:** a new persistent store, TTL/invalidation logic, and staleness-vs-freshness reasoning on a security-posture exporter. Net: **complexity ≫ benefit**.

### Recommendation

**Don't build a general local on-disk data cache.** The issue's own success criterion — *"in-process + a volume is enough"* — is the correct outcome, now backed by the code: there's no expensive recompute to avoid, no delta/ETag to make a cache safe, and the durable-progress need is already met by `CheckpointStore` + the #117/#118 restart handling.

**The one narrow, conditional candidate** (naming it so it's on record, not recommending it): persist *only the device-fleet snapshot* across restart — a scoped extension of `CachingFleetFetcher` reusing its already-accepted 30m TTL. It's the single piece of genuinely re-fetched **bulk** data. But on current evidence (tiny tenant, infrequent restarts, already cached in-process) it's not worth the code. Gate it on a **measured** restart-storm re-paging a large fleet, not build it speculatively.

- [x] Which reads/derived-state are expensive enough to persist — none clear the bar (no expensive recompute; expensive fetches are fresh-required or restart-covered)
- [x] Survive restarts usefully vs moot — moot (poll cadence + no delta/ETag ⇒ TTL-only, can't extend freshness)
- [x] CheckpointStore interaction — purpose-built for cursors; a data cache would fight it and should be separate, but isn't worth building
- [x] Net effect measured — bounded small savings vs real added complexity ⇒ decline

Closing as explored-and-declined (the pre-blessed successful outcome). Reopen if you want the scoped fleet-snapshot persistence — that's the only piece with any case, and only under a measured restart problem.
