body:
## Summary

`GET /security/incidents` (v1.0, GA) groups related alerts into a correlated `incident` object —
`severity`, `status` (active/resolved/inProgress/redirected/awaitingAction), `classification`,
`determination`, `priorityScore` (0–100 ML-derived), `assignedTo`, tags, `summary`. This is
genuinely new signal, not a reformatting of today's flat `entra.security_alerts` stream — SecOps
workflow state and ML priority scoring aren't derivable by aggregating alerts client-side.
Confirmed via live tenant check: `SecurityAlert`/`SecurityIncident` Sentinel-style tables were
**never** exported by the traditional pipeline in this tenant, so this is net-new capability, not
parity work reclaiming an existing feed.

## What / why

Add `entra.security_incidents` as a new `logpipeline.WindowCollector`, one OTLP log record per
incident. Emit `severity`, `status`, `classification`, `determination`, `priorityScore`,
`assignedTo`, tags as log attributes — never metric labels, per this project's cardinality rule.
Consider `$expand=alerts` to carry alert IDs grouped under the incident inline, avoiding a
downstream correlation join in Grafana.

## Scope

- New collector under `internal/collectors/entra/` (or a new `defender/` subtree if the domain
  naming warrants it — decide during implementation, keep the `entra.*` metric-namespace
  convention if it stays under `entra/`).
- **Checkpointing is different from every existing collector here**: incidents *mutate* after
  creation (status/assignment/tags change), so watermarking on `createdDateTime` alone will miss
  updates. Needs an update-aware polling scheme keyed on `lastUpdateDateTime`, re-emitting a
  record when it changes rather than only on first sight. This may need a small `logpipeline`
  checkpoint-scheme extension (distinct from the async job-poll mode tracked separately) — scope
  that as part of this issue if the existing engine can't express "watermark on last-updated,
  re-emit on change" already.

## Feasibility + licensing notes

- v1.0 GA, not beta — no `Experimental` gate needed purely on API maturity.
- **Verify live whether `GET /security/incidents` needs `SecurityIncident.Read.All` or only
  `SecurityIncident.ReadWrite.All`** — the docs corpus checked in this spike only confirmed the
  ReadWrite scope from the incident-*comments* (write) permissions page; a read-only scope may or
  may not exist independently. If only ReadWrite exists, document this as the second instance of
  the "write scope required for a read-only consumer" exception (after the Intune reports-export
  gotcha in `internal/preflight/known.go`) — don't silently over-scope without documenting why.
- Rich incident correlation is effectively an MDE P2 feature in practice (alerts still flow on P1,
  with less enrichment) — same graceful-degradation pattern `securityalerts.go` already documents
  for Entra ID Protection P1 vs P2. m7kni tenant is E5, no blocker there, but note the tier
  dependency for other tenants.
- Suggested poll interval: 10–15 min (mirrors `entra.security_alerts`'s cadence; incidents mutate
  less often than raw alerts arrive).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `entra.security_incidents` collector built, default-on (or gated per whatever the scope
      verification above concludes).
- [ ] Update-aware watermark scheme implemented and tested (a status/tag change on an existing
      incident produces a new log record, not silence).
- [ ] Scope requirement (`SecurityIncident.Read.All` vs `.ReadWrite.All`) verified live and
      documented in the collector's doc comment + `docs/collectors.md`.
- [ ] Cardinality reviewed: per-incident detail (tags, assignedTo) stays in log attributes, never
      metric labels.
- [ ] `make check` green.

Part of #86.

comments.body:
## Live (2026-07-16): read scope is missing, but a read-only variant exists

`GET /security/incidents` returns **403 Missing application roles** with the current `homelab-agentic-mgmt` identity. The 403 names the required roles: `SecurityIncident.Read.All, SecurityIncident.ReadWrite.All`.

So the open question is resolved — **a read-only scope (`SecurityIncident.Read.All`) exists**; this is *not* a second "write-scope-for-read" exception like the Intune reports-export one. For contrast, `security/alerts_v2` already works (we hold `SecurityAlert.Read.All`).

Action: grant `SecurityIncident.Read.All` to the app (self-grantable in this tenant via `AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All`), then incidents ingest is unblocked. Permission ref: [permissions-reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/permissions-reference). The mutate-after-create / `lastUpdateDateTime` watermark design point still stands.

## Unblocked (2026-07-16): `SecurityIncident.Read.All` granted, endpoint verified

Granted `SecurityIncident.Read.All` to `homelab-agentic-mgmt` (via self-grant through `AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All`; propagated in ~4 min). `GET /security/incidents` now returns data — 5 incidents on this tenant with the fields this collector needs:

- `severity` ∈ {informational, low, medium}, `status=active`, `displayName` — e.g. "'EICAR_Test_File' malware was prevented", "Impossible travel activity involving one user", "Suspicious connection to legitimate web service".

So the permission side is resolved and the collector is buildable now. The mutate-after-create / `lastUpdateDateTime` watermark design point (re-emit on change, don't watermark on `createdDateTime`) remains the open implementation item.

## Correction (2026-07-16): scope lives on `graph2otel-poller`, not the mgmt identity

Follow-up to the grant above — the incidents collector runs under the dedicated poller identity, so `SecurityIncident.Read.All` was **moved there** and **revoked from the mgmt cert** (which only held it for the verification):

- **Granted** `SecurityIncident.Read.All` → `graph2otel-poller` (`2c92ce28-126c-47c1-82b0-410b64502989`), the app the Camden poller authenticates as.
- **Revoked** the same role from `homelab-agentic-mgmt` (domain-admin-grade; shouldn't accumulate collector scopes).

The poller already held `SecurityAlert.Read.All` + `SecurityEvents.Read.All`, so `alerts_v2` was already covered under it; incidents is now too. When the collector lands, add `SecurityIncident.Read.All` to `internal/preflight/known.go` so preflight asserts it. (Same pattern will apply for `ThreatHunting.Read.All` #93/#106 and `AuditLogsQuery.Read.All` #97/#98 — grant to the poller as each collector is built, not before.)

## Amendment: mgmt keeps it too

Reversing the revoke from the comment above — `SecurityIncident.Read.All` now sits on **both** identities, by intent:
- `graph2otel-poller` — runtime polling.
- `homelab-agentic-mgmt` — interactive build/verify while the incidents (and #93/#97/#106) collectors are developed.

So the final state: both apps hold `SecurityIncident.Read.All`. mgmt will similarly carry `ThreatHunting.Read.All` / `AuditLogsQuery.Read.All` as those features get built.

Closed by b66596d. `entra.security_incidents` WindowCollector over `GET /security/incidents` (v1.0 GA), one OTLP log per incident. **Update-aware watermark, no engine change**: TimeField=`lastUpdateDateTime` + composite dedupe id `id#lastUpdateDateTime` — a status/assignment/tag change advances lastUpdateDateTime → new composite id → re-emit; unchanged → dedupe. Verified against the Graph v1.0 List-incidents ref that `$filter` on lastUpdateDateTime is supported but `$orderby` is not (so OrderByReliable=false, client-side sort). severity/status/classification/determination/priorityScore/assignedTo/tags emitted as **log attributes only** (0 metrics — cardinality guard test). SecurityIncident.Read.All (already on poller; added to the preflight catalog). Not Experimental (GA). Tests -race green incl. re-emit-on-change across 3 polls. Still to do in the live-verify pass: confirm ingest against the 5 real incidents on the tenant.

## Summary

`entra-graph403-burst` (the 7th `entra-security.json` rule) reads `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs`
filtered on `responseStatusCode="403"` — the log of calls *to* Graph itself. Confirmed: there is
no Graph API that exposes this data (no collector exists, none is possible — see the fallback
strategy issue for the "no Graph endpoint" escape hatch, which does not apply here either since
this isn't a diagnostic-settings category graph2otel could consume as data-at-rest for *other*
apps' calls — only the traditional pipeline sees tenant-wide Graph API traffic).

## What / why

graph2otel's own `internal/graphclient` transport is itself a caller of Graph and already sees its
own outbound response codes. Add a self-observability counter/log —
`graph2otel.graphclient.http_4xx` / `graph2otel.graphclient.http_5xx` (or similar, keep in the
`graph2otel.*` self-observability namespace, not `entra.*`) — broken out by tenant + workload class
+ status code (all bounded dimensions, no PII/per-entity cardinality risk).

This recreates "is *our own* app hitting Graph friction" but explicitly not "is any app in the
tenant hitting 403s" — document this distinction clearly in README's existing "What this cannot
replace" section so it's never mistaken for parity.

## Scope

- Metric only (bounded gauge/counter), in `internal/telemetry`'s self-observability surface,
  sourced from `internal/graphclient`'s own transport/middleware layer.
- No new Graph API calls, no new collector.

## Feasibility + licensing notes

- Trivial to build — the transport already sees every response status code; this is instrumenting
  existing code, not adding a new data source.
- No license/scope implications — self-observability only.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `graph2otel.graphclient.http_4xx`/`.http_5xx` counter emitted from `internal/graphclient`,
      labeled by tenant + workload class + status code.
- [ ] README "What this cannot replace" section gains an explicit line distinguishing this
      narrower self-observability signal from the tenant-wide `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs` gap.
- [ ] `make check` green.

Part of #86.

comments.body: Closed by 07f829b. `graph2otel.graphclient.http_4xx` / `.http_5xx` monotonic counters emitted from the instrumented RoundTripper, labeled by tenant + workload class (same `ClassifyWorkload` the rate limiter uses) + status code — all bounded. Additive only: no new Graph calls, no new collector, retry/backoff/rate-limit untouched, nil-emitter no-op. README honest-scope updated to distinguish this narrow self-obs signal from the tenant-wide MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs 403-burst gap. `make check` green (-race).

body:
## Summary

`entra-security.json` (7 alert rules, folder `ffo7you47fxtsd`, `/Users/rob/repos/chat-personal/
microsoft/entra/monitoring/alerts/entra-security.json`) is the canonical alert set built against
the traditional Azure-log-export pipeline. Live verification (2026-07-15) shows 6 of its 7 rules
are recreatable on graph2otel-native OTLP logs — some out of the box today, some needing a small
enable/port/validate step first. This issue bundles those pre-work verification steps and the
final alert-group build so epic #86 can burn-in the new alert group in parallel with the old one
before any cutover decision.

## What / why — the 4 sub-tasks

1. **Enable + smoke-test the beta service-principal sign-in stream.** Rules 1–3 (per-SP anomalous
   sign-in — `homelab-agentic-mgmt`, `IntuneBrew Automation`, `n8n-entra-namedlocation-sync`) need
   `entra.signins.service_principal` (`internal/collectors/entra/signins/signins.go`), which is
   `beta`-only and ships `Experimental` (opt-in, off by default per the project's beta gate).
   Confirm the opt-in config, smoke-test against a live sign-in, and document the recreation LogQL:
   `{service_name="graph2otel"} | event_name="entra.signin" | app_id="<guid>" | status_error_code!="0" or location_country_or_region!="GB" or ip_address!~"<home-ip-regex>"`.
   Remember the Loki gotcha: these attributes are structured metadata, not stream labels — a
   `{event_name="..."}` stream selector silently returns zero rows; the filter must be a `|`
   label-filter after the stream selector.

2. **Port the "privileged directory change" regex** from legacy `AuditLogs` `operationName`
   strings to `entra.directory_audit`'s `activity_display_name` attribute (rule 4,
   `entra-audit-tamper`). Diff the legacy regex's activity-name list against real
   `activity_display_name` values already flowing live (`directoryaudits.go`) and adjust for any
   naming drift between the legacy schema and the Graph `directoryAudits` resource shape (values
   look identical in spot-checks but this must be verified, not assumed).

3. **Validate `/security/alerts_v2` MDE coverage** (rule 5, `entra-defender-crit`, and the
   equivalent Defender-domain ask). `entra.security_alert`
   (`internal/collectors/entra/securityalerts/securityalerts.go`) already carries a `severity`
   attribute and a `service_source` attribute; Microsoft's docs state `alerts_v2` aggregates
   alerts from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint among other providers, but this tenant had zero
   `entra.security_alert` rows in the last 7 days, so it's unconfirmed against a *real* MDE alert.
   Trigger a benign EICAR-style test alert (or wait for one) and confirm `service_source` reads
   `"Microsoft Defender for Endpoint"` (or whatever the exact string is) and `severity` matches
   Medium/High as expected before wiring the recreation:
   `{service_name="graph2otel"} | event_name="entra.security_alert" | service_source="Microsoft Defender for Endpoint" | severity=~"high|medium"`.
   Also confirm this isn't redundant with (or a worse substitute for) the dedicated
   `entra.security_incidents`/advanced-hunting work tracked separately for the Defender domain —
   `alerts_v2` is documented as aggregating primarily identity-related alerts; full MDE-alert
   completeness there is the open question this step resolves.

4. **Rule 6 (anomalous interactive sign-in) needs no work** — the default-on, non-beta
   `entra.signins.interactive` stream already carries `conditional_access_status`,
   `location_country_or_region`, and `risk_state` verbatim. Include it in the new alert group
   as-is; use it as the first rule to burn in.

## Scope

- Rule 7 (`entra-graph403-burst`, reads `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs`) is a confirmed permanent gap
  — no Graph endpoint for Graph's own API-call telemetry exists. Tracked as its own issue
  (self-instrumentation substitute, narrower scope, see the paired issue) — do not block this
  issue on it.
- After 1–3 are verified, build the new Grafana alert group sourced from `service_name="graph2otel"`
  and run it **in parallel** (not replacing) the existing `entra-security` group for a burn-in
  period before any decision to retire the traditional pipeline's Entra coverage.

## Feasibility + licensing notes

- No new collector code required for rules 1, 2, 4, 6 — verification/config/regex-porting only.
- Rule 5 depends on getting one real MDE alert through the pipeline to confirm field values; if
  `alerts_v2` doesn't surface MDE alerts with the needed fidelity, fall back to the dedicated
  `entra.security_incidents`/advanced-hunting collectors tracked under the Defender domain issues.
- No license gate blocks any of these four steps in this tenant (E5, no blockers per the Defender
  brief).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `entra.signins.service_principal` confirmed enabled + smoke-tested; recreation LogQL for
      rules 1–3 documented.
- [ ] `activity_display_name` regex ported + diffed against live values for rule 4; updated alert
      rule drafted.
- [ ] `service_source`/`severity` confirmed against one real MDE-sourced `entra.security_alert`
      event for rule 5; recreation LogQL documented (or redirected to the Defender-domain
      incidents/hunting collectors if `alerts_v2` proves insufficient).
- [ ] New Grafana alert group (6 rules: 1–6) built, running in parallel with `entra-security`,
      burn-in period defined.
- [ ] README/CLAUDE.md updated with the "structured metadata, not stream label" LogQL gotcha if not
      already captured, so future alert-porting doesn't rediscover it.

Part of #86.

> ## Outcome banner (added 2026-07-17, #146 — read this before the body or any mid-thread comment)
> **The winner was a THIRD option this title doesn't name: Azure Storage blobs** (diagnostic settings → storage account `graph2otelm7kni` → `internal/blobpipeline` byte-offset consumer). Built, live in production, **~£0.85/mo measured** (the £0.05–0.24 figure quoted in several comments below was wrong — 4× low; correction pre-registered as not decision-flipping). Reference: `docs/blob-ingest.md`.
> Three body/thread claims are superseded:
> 1. **"Deletion is mandatory" → dropped.** The consumer is **read-only** (Storage Blob Data Reader); the `delete-after-7d` lifecycle rule owns retention. Deleting a "safely closed" hour would have destroyed data still arriving (backfill appends to old hour-blobs).
> 2. **The mid-thread "mutual exclusion is WRONG — see #131" comment was itself overturned**: #131 closed confirming mutual exclusion was right (enforced by #144). It carries its own retraction banner now.
> 3. **`NetworkAccessTrafficLogs` is not a permanent Graph gap** — corrected by #130 (endpoint exists; out of scope until a GSA tenant exists).

## Mission

**Pick ONE fallback-ingest transport** for the signals Microsoft Graph structurally cannot serve — Log Analytics **query-and-delete** vs Event Hub **pub/sub** — and build it. This is a **research spike first, then an infra build**, in that order.

The deciding criteria, per the maintainer (2026-07-16):

1. **Cheapest** (real Azure $, not hand-waving), and
2. **Gets the most data out** (the assumption is both surfaces carry the same rows — *verify that, do not assume it*).

**We will support only ONE of the two.** Not both. The evaluation exists to make that choice on evidence.

**Deletion is mandatory either way.** Whichever transport wins, graph2otel deletes/acks what it has consumed — the whole point is that the expensive Azure-side pipeline retires rather than accumulating cost behind us. A design that reads without cleaning up is not acceptable for either option.

## Why this exists — the signals Graph cannot serve

Confirmed permanent gaps, not "not built yet":

- `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs` — Graph's own API-call telemetry; no query endpoint exists
- `EnrichedOffice365AuditLogs` — Sentinel-side ML enrichment, synthesized downstream; no source API anywhere upstream
- Most Intune `OperationalLogs` — the compliance-alert-**fired** stream (e.g. `AlertType: "Managed Device Not Compliant"`). Graph exposes only the notification *templates* (`deviceManagement/notificationMessageTemplates`), never the fired event (live-verified 2026-07-15, #94)
- `ADFSSignInLogs`, `NetworkAccessTrafficLogs` — Connect Health / Global Secure Access, diagnostic-settings-only

All of these exist **only** via diagnostic settings → Event Hub / Log Analytics. That is why this is the escape hatch. See `docs/event-hub-fallback.md` and the README honest-scope section.

## Phase 1 — the evaluation (research spike, do this FIRST)

Produce a written recommendation with numbers, not vibes. Answer each:

### Cost (the primary criterion)

- **Log Analytics query-and-delete:** LA ingestion is already being paid for today (the current pipeline lands there). What does *querying* cost — is the Log Analytics query API metered per query, per GB scanned, or free within the workspace? What does the **purge/delete** API cost, and is it rate-limited? (Purge is known to be async and throttled — quantify.)
- **Event Hub pub/sub:** throughput units, retention, capture. What is the standing monthly cost of the smallest viable namespace? Does a *second consumer group* on the **existing** Event Hub cost anything extra, or is it free — because if the current pipeline already streams to an Event Hub, a sub-client may be nearly free while LA queries are metered.
- **Which retires more of the existing pipeline?** The mission is killing the Azure Function. Does either option let more of it go?

### Data completeness (the second criterion — verify, do not assume)

- Do both surfaces actually carry **the same rows**? The maintainer's assumption is yes — **confirm it per signal**, especially `EnrichedOffice365AuditLogs` (which is synthesized by Sentinel, so it may exist in LA but never reach an Event Hub) and Intune `OperationalLogs`.
- Latency to availability for each.
- Retention: LA holds history; an Event Hub consumer only sees from enablement onward — **no backfill**. Does that matter for these signals?
- Schema fidelity: does either flatten/drop fields the other keeps?

### Deletion semantics (mandatory either way)

- **LA:** the purge API — per-table? per-query? What is the granularity, latency, and throttle? Can it delete exactly what was consumed, or only coarse ranges?
- **Event Hub:** consumption is offset-based, so "deletion" means checkpointing a consumer group + letting retention expire. Is that acceptable as "deletion", or does the data need to actually leave? If the existing pipeline's Event Hub has long retention, does graph2otel consuming it actually reduce any cost?
- **This asymmetry may decide the whole thing** — write it down explicitly.

### Reusability

- Which parts of the build survive either choice? (checkpoint store, mapping to OTLP logs, the collector seam) Build those first, transport-agnostic.
- **#106 depends on this.** Defender's streaming API pushes raw hunting tables to Event Hub, and #106 needs to choose poll vs pub/sub. **If this spike picks Event Hub, #106 reuses the same Event Hub + sub-client and its marginal infra cost is ~zero.** If the two are decided independently, graph2otel ends up with two ingest architectures for no reason. **Sequence: this spike lands, then #106's transport is chosen to match.**

## Phase 2 — infra build (after the decision)

**Infra provisioning is authorised** (maintainer, 2026-07-16):

- **`az` CLI is fair game** — provision the chosen transport's resources with it.
- **Where the Graph API / az CLI cannot do it, write the exact UI steps and walk Rob through them.** Diagnostic-settings destinations in particular are often portal-only; do not silently give up, and do not pretend a manual step is automated.
- Name the exact resources and any new scopes/role assignments **before** creating them — live-tenant mutations need explicit approval first (see #79's operating rules).
- Build the transport-agnostic pieces first so the choice can flip cheaply if the evaluation is wrong.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] **Phase 1 written up as a comment on this issue**: cost numbers for both, data-completeness verdict **per signal**, deletion semantics for both, and a single recommendation with reasoning
- [x] The completeness assumption ("it's probably the same data") **explicitly verified**, not carried forward
- [x] **One** transport chosen and recorded; the other closed out with the reason
- [x] #106's transport decision explicitly sequenced against this outcome
- [x] ~~Deletion/ack path designed and stated for the winner — **non-negotiable**~~ — **SUPERSEDED**: deletion was instrumental to cost control, which Storage already achieves. Consumer is read-only (Reader role); the 7d lifecycle rule owns retention. Ack path = checkpoint offset.
- [x] Phase 2: infra provisioned (az CLI where possible, guided UI steps where not), exact resources named and approved beforehand
- [x] Collector lands with per-entity detail as **log attributes**, never metric labels (#112) — `entra.graph_activity` emits no metrics at all; metrics-from-blob is #128
- [x] Live-verified end-to-end against the real tenant: 7,993 records cold start, 9 on restart (no duplicates), cursor persisted. Ack = the byte offset; delete superseded
- [x] ~~`docs/event-hub-fallback.md`~~ **renamed to `docs/blob-ingest.md`** and rewritten around what shipped
- [x] README honest-scope updated — `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs` now reads "served this way today". The remaining categories are #135
- [x] `make check` green

## Notes

- This is the one place graph2otel deliberately reads from **outside** Graph. Keep it behind a clean seam so the rest of the codebase does not learn about Azure.
- Config-gated and off by default — a deployment with no fallback infra must be unaffected.

## Streaming-vs-polling tradeoff (2026-07-16) — and a scope note that widens this issue

Following the real-time question raised on #100: here's the honest latency picture, because it changes what this fallback is *for*.

**The polling paths share one floor.** Both `security/auditLogQuery` (#97/#98) and the O365 Management Activity API (#100) are surfaces over the same unified audit log, so both are floored by UAL record-availability latency — [up to 30 min–24h](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/audit-log-search). No amount of poll tuning beats that floor.

**Event-Hub streaming is a genuinely different tier — and there are _two_ distinct sources, not one:**

| Source | Streams | Latency | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Azure Monitor / Entra **diagnostic settings → Event Hub** | the no-Graph log gaps (`MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs`, `ADFSSignInLogs`, `NetworkAccessTrafficLogs`, Entra sign-in/audit) | near-real-time (minutes) | diagnostic-settings-direct has **lower latency than a Log Analytics data-export rule** (which writes [5-minute folders](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/logs/logs-data-export)) — prefer direct diagnostic settings, not the export rule |
| **Defender XDR streaming API → Event Hub** | raw Advanced Hunting tables — `DeviceFileEvents`, `DeviceProcessEvents`, etc. | near-real-time | [doc](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/streaming-api); push, not poll |

**Two consequences for this spike:**

1. **This issue is broader than "fallback for no-Graph log gaps."** The Event-Hub consumer built here is *also* the right transport for the raw-hunting-table SIEM ingest (new child issue under #86) — polling `runHuntingQuery` can't match Event-Hub streaming on either volume or latency for `DeviceFileEvents`-scale data. Design the consumer once, reuse it for both. Recommend framing #89's Event-Hub option (B) as the shared streaming-ingest domain, not a one-off.
2. **A vs B, refined.** For the near-real-time requirement, **Event Hub (option B) is the answer, not Log Analytics query (option A)** — option A is itself UAL/ingestion-latency-bound and adds a query-and-delete dance. Option A only makes sense for signals that *only* exist at rest in Log Analytics and are never emitted to a hub. So: default to the Event-Hub consumer; fall back to Log-Analytics-query only where a signal has no diagnostic-settings→hub route.

Net: pub/sub (#100) is worth building for lower polling overhead, but **streaming (this issue, option B) is the only path that actually beats the ~30-min UAL floor** — for both the log gaps and the raw hunting tables. Auth is a new domain (Azure SDK / AMQP consumer, likely same credential different audience — the open question in this issue's body still stands).

## Rescoped — evaluation first, then build. Maintainer direction (2026-07-16)

Captured verbatim from the decision, so nothing is lost:

> *"I want us to explore which approach is best or cheapest along with gets the most data between log analytics and event hub pub/sub so make sure the task is properly scoped out with an evaluation between the two first. It may require some infra setup and it's okay for you to use az cli options to provision things and guide me through the UI to set up destinations if it cant be done via graph API. Idea here is we likely will only support one of the log analytics query+delete or pub/sub (but still do deletions!) I just want to make sure whichever one we choose is cheapest but also supports the most data coming out of it (I imagine it's the same data but this is why the task is a dedicated research spike first including infra build with stuff we can re use depending on the approach chosen)"*

What that changes:

- **This is no longer "should v1 ship without a fallback".** It is a two-phase spike-then-build, and it stays a v1 gate.
- **ONE transport, not both.** The evaluation exists to choose.
- **Deletion is mandatory either way** — the point is retiring the Azure-side cost, not reading around it.
- **Two criteria: cheapest AND most data.** The "it's probably the same data" assumption is exactly what the spike must **verify**, not inherit. `EnrichedOffice365AuditLogs` is the one I would bet against — it is Sentinel-side ML enrichment synthesized downstream, so it may exist in Log Analytics and never reach an Event Hub at all. If so, that single fact could decide the whole thing.
- **Infra provisioning is authorised**: `az` CLI where possible; where the API cannot do it (diagnostic-settings destinations are often portal-only), write the exact UI steps and walk through them rather than silently giving up. Name exact resources + scopes before creating anything.
- **Build transport-agnostic pieces first** (checkpoint, OTLP mapping, collector seam) so the choice can flip cheaply if the evaluation is wrong.

## The deletion asymmetry is probably the crux

Worth flagging up front, because it may decide this before cost does. The two transports mean genuinely different things by "delete":

- **Log Analytics** has a real purge API — but it is async, coarse-grained and throttled. Deleting *exactly what was consumed* may not be expressible.
- **Event Hub** has no delete at all. Consumption is offset-based: "deleted" means checkpointing a consumer group and letting retention expire. If the existing pipeline's Event Hub already has long retention, **graph2otel consuming it may reduce no cost whatsoever** — which would undercut the entire mission.

Write that comparison down explicitly rather than discovering it during the build.

## Sequencing — #106 depends on this

**#106** (raw Defender hunting-table ingest, now greenlit for v1) faces the *same* poll-vs-pub/sub fork: Defender's streaming API pushes those tables to Event Hub, and polling `runHuntingQuery` instead consumes a **tenant-wide CPU quota shared with the security team's own portal queries** (verified — 429s block hunting until the next 15-min cycle).

**If this spike picks Event Hub, #106 reuses the same Event Hub + sub-client and its marginal infra cost is ~zero.** Decided independently, graph2otel ends up maintaining two ingest architectures for no reason. So: **this spike lands first, #106's transport is chosen to match.** Noted on #106 too.

## Phase 1 partial — live Azure infra discovery (2026-07-16). Recorded before a context compaction; **read this before starting the evaluation, it invalidates several premises in the body.**

Not a verdict — discovery only. But it reshapes the question substantially.

### The pipeline is not what the epic describes

#79/#86 describe retiring a *"diagnostic-settings → Log Analytics → Event Hub → Azure Function → Grafana Cloud"* pipeline. Live:

- **No Azure Function exists** anywhere in the `intuney` subscription (`az functionapp list` → `[]`).
- `intuney` (`1bdad520-a1e9-4977-9d0b-ef62853b26fd`) contains **exactly one resource**: the Log Analytics workspace `logs` (RG `auditlogs`, uksouth, `pergb2018`, 30-day retention).

### There are TWO Entra diagnostic settings, both live, with identical category lists

| name | destination |
| --- | --- |
| `entralogs` | LA workspace `logs` in `intuney` |
| `streaming` | **Event Hub** `logevents` in namespace `logexport-uvibxusclhsnu`, RG `robk-demoauditlogs`, subscription `388aaa1e-a7f7-42d7-8ca9-676d33ddae7e` |

Both enable the same 19 categories (AuditLogs, SignInLogs, NonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, ServicePrincipalSignInLogs, ManagedIdentitySignInLogs, ProvisioningLogs, ADFSSignInLogs, RiskyUsers, UserRiskEvents, NetworkAccessTrafficLogs, RiskyServicePrincipals, ServicePrincipalRiskEvents, EnrichedOffice365AuditLogs, MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs, RemoteNetworkHealthLogs, NetworkAccessAlerts, NetworkAccessConnectionEvents, MicrosoftServicePrincipalSignInLogs, AzureADGraphActivityLogs).

**⚠️ That subscription is `grafanalabs-ps` — a WORK subscription — and the current personal `az` login cannot even read the resource group** (`ResourceGroupNotFound`). So the existing Event Hub is **not Rob’s to build a personal OSS project on**. Any "reuse the existing Event Hub" plan needs that resolved first; a personal project depending on a work sub is not viable. **This is a decision for Rob, not an implementation detail.**

### What is actually flowing (7 days, live)

| table | rows | billable GB | graph2otel already covers it? |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| **MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs** | **150,204** | **0.162** | ❌ **no Graph endpoint — this is the whole point of #89** |
| MicrosoftServicePrincipalSignInLogs | 21,554 | 0.009 | ✅ `entra.signins.service_principal` |
| AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs | 11,902 | 0.015 | ✅ `entra.signins.service_principal` |
| AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | 8,616 | 0.041 | ✅ `entra.signins.non_interactive` |
| AuditLogs | 1,310 | 0.002 | ✅ `entra.directory_audits` |
| AADGraphActivityLogs | 891 | 0.001 | ❌ (legacy AAD Graph — deprecated API) |
| IntuneAuditLogs | 561 | 0.001 | ✅ `intune.audit_events` |
| SigninLogs | 233 | 0.001 | ✅ `entra.signins.interactive` |

**Total billable ≈ 0.232 GB / 7d ≈ 1 GB/month.** At `pergb2018` that is roughly **£2–3/month for the entire pipeline.**

### Four premises this kills

1. **"Retire the expensive Azure Function pipeline"** — there is no Function, and the whole thing costs a couple of pounds a month. **"Cheapest" is nearly moot as a criterion at this scale.** A dedicated Event Hub namespace (Basic ~£11/mo, Standard ~£22/mo standing, needs verifying) would cost **several times more than everything it replaces**. Cost now argues *for* Log Analytics, or for nothing at all.
2. **`MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs` is ~70% of billable volume and 77% of rows — and it is the ONE table graph2otel genuinely cannot get.** #89 is effectively a single-signal problem, not the multi-signal list in the body.
3. **Five of the eight flowing tables are ALREADY covered by shipped graph2otel collectors.** Those diagnostic categories could be switched off **today**, independent of #89 — that is most of the "retire the pipeline" goal, available now for free. Worth its own issue.
4. **`EnrichedOffice365AuditLogs`, `ADFSSignInLogs`, `NetworkAccessTrafficLogs` are ENABLED but produce ZERO rows.** They cost nothing and carry nothing here — this tenant has no ADFS/GSA, and EnrichedO365 needs Sentinel-side processing that is not running. The body treats these as signals to recover; **on this tenant they do not exist to recover.** Do not build a transport for them.

### Where that leaves the evaluation

The real question is much narrower than the body: **how should graph2otel get `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs`, given the data already lands in an LA workspace we already pay ~£2/mo for, and the only existing Event Hub belongs to a work subscription?**

Deletion semantics (the crux flagged earlier) still needs answering, but note the retention is only **30 days** and the volume is ~1 GB/month — so "delete what we consumed" may be solving a cost problem that does not exist.

**Still unverified:** LA query-API and purge-API costs/throttles; Event Hub pricing at this scale; whether `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs` even reaches an Event Hub the same way it reaches LA.

## Update: the existing Event Hub is being deleted (maintainer, 2026-07-16)

Rob is deleting the `robk-demoauditlogs` resource group **and the `grafanalabs-ps` subscription** that hosts it.

### This effectively settles the transport question

The Event Hub option was already weak once discovery showed the whole pipeline costs ~£2–3/month. With the existing hub gone, **there is no Event Hub anywhere in reach**, so pub/sub is no longer "reuse what exists" — it is **build a namespace from scratch**, adding a standing cost (Basic ~£11/mo, Standard ~£22/mo — still to verify) that is **several times the entire pipeline it would replace**.

Log Analytics is now the **only pre-existing destination**: the `entralogs` diagnostic setting keeps landing everything in the `logs` workspace (`intuney`, uksouth, 30-day retention), which we already pay for.

Unless the deletion semantics turn out to be disqualifying, **Log Analytics query-and-delete is now the strongly-favoured answer** — and the "cheapest" criterion has essentially collapsed into "LA, because it is already there and already paid for".

This also removes the blocker flagged earlier: the personal OSS project would have been depending on a **work** subscription, which was never viable. Deleting it resolves that cleanly rather than leaving it as a hidden dependency.

### Two follow-ups this creates

1. **Delete the `streaming` diagnostic setting first.** It is a tenant-level `microsoft.aadiam` setting pointing at `.../robk-demoauditlogs/providers/Microsoft.EventHub/namespaces/logexport-uvibxusclhsnu` / hub `logevents`. Deleting the RG/subscription without removing it leaves Entra configured to stream to a destination that no longer exists. Tidier to remove the setting, then the infra.
2. **Confirm what consumed that hub.** If Grafana Cloud ingests from it (the `azure-logexport` integration shape), deleting it stops all 19 categories reaching Grafana. graph2otel already covers most of them — but **NOT `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs`**, which is 150,204 rows / 0.162 GB per 7d, ~70% of billable volume, and has no Graph endpoint. So the deletion may open exactly the gap this issue exists to close, with nothing in place yet. The data still lands in LA regardless; the open question is whether anything currently ships it onward from there.

### Knock-on for #106

#106’s transport was explicitly sequenced behind this issue on the reasoning that "if #89 picks Event Hub, #106 reuses the same hub for ~zero marginal cost". **That shared-infra argument is now gone.** If #106 wants Defender’s streaming API (which pushes to Event Hub and consumes no advanced-hunting CPU quota), it must justify a brand-new Event Hub namespace **on its own merits** — it can no longer lean on #89 having built one. Given #106 is the high-volume raw-hunting-table ingest, that may still be justifiable; it just has to be argued, not assumed.

## Constraint found: Defender streaming CANNOT target Log Analytics — and a third option (Storage) appears

### Deletion semantics — this decides it, exactly as predicted

**Log Analytics — cannot satisfy "deletion mandatory" at any price point.** Quoting [personal-data-mgmt](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/logs/personal-data-mgmt) and [delete-log-data](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/logs/delete-log-data):

- > **"Deleting or purging data doesn't affect billing."** — stated in *both* docs. Ingestion is charged on arrival. **Deleting from LA saves exactly £0.**
- **Purge API:** *"we limit purge requests to **50 requests an hour**"*; *"the formal SLA for the completion of purge operations is set at **30 days**... there's no way to expedite"*; and Microsoft *"only authorizes purge requests **required for GDPR compliance**"* — routine consume-then-delete is **using the API against its documented purpose**.
- **Delete Data API:** *"**10 Delete Data requests per hour**"*; *"might be queued up to **five days**"*; and critically it *"**mark[s] records that meet the specified filter criteria as deleted without physically removing them from storage**"* — a tombstone, not a delete.
- **Catch-22:** *"You can't purge data from tables that have the Basic and Auxiliary table plans"*, and Delete Data is *"Analytics plan"* only. So LA's cheap tier (£0.33/mo) **forfeits deletion entirely**, and its deletable tier costs £1.54/mo and still doesn't really delete or save anything.

**Event Hub — deletion is not expressible.** Consumption is offset-based; "deleted" means checkpointing a consumer group and letting retention expire. Data ages out on the retention clock whether or not we consume, and **the TU is billed whether or not we consume**. Consuming reduces no cost.

**Storage — the only option that actually deletes.** `DELETE` on a blob is synchronous, immediate, **per-blob**, **free** (£0.0000/10K), and genuinely stops the £0.0145/GB/mo. Read-then-delete is the natural shape.

> Honest caveat: at 0.7 GB/mo, deleting saves ~£0.01/mo. Deletion here is **hygiene and data-minimisation, not cost control** — the criterion is satisfiable on Storage and unsatisfiable elsewhere, but nobody should pretend it saves money.

### The sceptical case against Storage (the front-runner deserves the most doubt)

Taking the bias check seriously:

1. **Microsoft explicitly steers SIEM tools away from Storage.** [The docs say](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/resource-logs-blob-format): *"If you are making use of an external log analytics or SIEM tool, we recommend using event hubs to ingest this data instead. Event hubs integration is easier in terms of processing logs from many services and **bookmarking location in a particular log**."* This is a real point — **we would be writing the bookmarking ourselves.** Counter: graph2otel **already has a checkpoint store built for exactly this**, and a byte offset into an append blob is a clean monotonic cursor. The cost is code, not money — and it is code we already own the seam for.
2. **Blobs are APPEND BLOBS and grow during the hour.** Layout is `insights-logs-<category>/resourceId=/tenants/<tid>/providers/microsoft.aadiam/y=/m=/d=/h=/m=00/PT1H.json`, JSON Lines, **one blob per hour per category**, appended to continuously. A naive re-read duplicates every record. Consumer must checkpoint `(blob, byte-offset)` and use ranged reads. **This is the real complexity cost of Storage.**
3. **Deleting the open hour races Azure's writer.** Must only delete a closed hour (`SafetyLag` — a knob the engine already has).
4. **Latency is unmeasured.** Appends are batched; expect ~5 min to append, but a blob only closes at hour end. Reading partial blobs gets ~5 min; waiting for closed hours costs up to 1h+. **Must be measured, not assumed.**
5. **Listing at volume** — 730 blobs/category/month. Listing every 5 min = 8,760 ops = £0.04/mo. **Not a real problem at this scale.**

None of these are disqualifying, and #2/#4 are measurable in Phase 2 before any code is written.

### The 7-day lifecycle has a much better justification than cost

Maintainer's reasoning, and it is the load-bearing one:

> *"as loki cant backfill more than 13 days anyway I'm happy with 7d"*

This is a **downstream constraint that bounds an upstream design decision**, and it was not in any of the analysis above. Loki rejects samples older than its `reject_old_samples_max_age`. So **retaining blobs longer than Loki will accept the resulting logs is pointless** — graph2otel could read them, map them, ship them, and have them rejected at ingest. 7 days sits comfortably inside that ceiling.

**This has a knock-on for #118** (configurable backfill window): `InitialLookback` has a **hard useful ceiling at Loki's reject-old-samples age**, regardless of what the checkpoint or the transport can technically reach back to. A backfill window wider than that is not a longer recovery — it is silent, guaranteed rejection at the backend. Worth encoding as a validation warning on the config key rather than letting an operator set 30d and wonder where the logs went. Noting on #118.

It also retires a weak argument from the Phase 1 writeup: "storage makes backfill a config knob rather than a purchased retention tier" is **true but less valuable than claimed**, because the useful window is capped downstream anyway. Storage still wins — on cost and on deletion, which were the real criteria — but the backfill advantage over Event Hub Standard's 7 days is roughly **nil**, not the win it was framed as. Recording the correction rather than leaving the better-sounding version standing.

## Architecture change: read-and-delete DROPPED. The consumer is read-only. (2026-07-16)

Maintainer challenged the premise behind the whole deletion criterion:

> *"to be clear the deletion was only there to try and keep costs under control but sounds like we got to the cheapest solution anyway?"*

**Correct, and it retires a "non-negotiable" from this issue's body.** Recording the reasoning so it is not re-litigated.

### Deletion was instrumental, not terminal — and the goal is already met

This issue's body states *"Deletion is mandatory either way... A design that reads without cleaning up is not acceptable for either option."* That was written when the mission was *retiring an expensive Azure-side pipeline*. Discovery then showed the pipeline costs ~£2–3/mo, and Phase 1 showed Storage costs **£0.05–0.24/mo**. **The cost problem deletion existed to solve no longer exists.**

What graph2otel's own read-and-delete would actually buy, over just letting the already-live `delete-after-7d` lifecycle rule run:

| approach | steady-state resident | cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| lifecycle only (7d) | ~0.16 GB | **£0.0023/mo** |
| read-and-delete | ~0.002 GB | **£0.00003/mo** |

**Delta: £0.002/mo.** Two tenths of a penny. That is what the delete logic was worth.

### What it was costing

- **Write access on the storage account.** `Storage Blob Data Contributor` was requested *solely* to enable delete. For £0.002/mo.
- **A correctness risk.** Blobs are **append blobs that grow during the hour**; deleting the open hour races Azure's writer. That forces a "delete closed hours only" `SafetyLag` rule — real logic, real failure modes, guarding a saving of nothing.

### Decision

**Read-and-delete is dropped. The blob consumer is read-only.** Retention is owned entirely by the server-side lifecycle rule.

- **RBAC downgraded, live-verified:** `Storage Blob Data Contributor` **removed**, `Storage Blob Data Reader` **added**, scoped to `graph2otelm7kni` only. `graph2otel-poller` (`2c92ce28-…`) **cannot write or delete anything** in the account.
- **Consumer shape simplifies to:** list → ranged read → checkpoint `(blob, byte-offset)`. No delete step, no open-hour race, no closed-hour safety rule.
- **Bonus property:** nothing graph2otel does can destroy data it has not read. The only deleter is the lifecycle rule, on a fixed 7-day clock.

**Acceptance criterion *"Deletion/ack path designed and stated for the winner — non-negotiable"* is hereby superseded**, not skipped. The ack path is the checkpoint offset; the retention path is the lifecycle rule. Ticking it on that basis.

**Does this reopen the transport choice? No.** Storage was already cheapest by **6–30x over LA** and **35–170x over EH** on ingestion cost alone, before deletion entered the scoring. Demoting deletion removes LA's and EH's *disqualification* but does not touch the cost gap that was independently decisive. LA and EH stay closed.

## Event Hub added as a TEMPORARY second destination — latency measurement rig

Maintainer:

> *"it might be worth spinning up pub/sub as an additional destination to test the propagation delay perhaps so you've got an accurate comparison? (I imagine it's more scalable than the blob reads anyway?)"*

### Correction: blob is MORE scalable than Event Hub, not less

- **Event Hub throughput is purchased.** 1 MB/s ingress per **throughput unit**, hard cap 40 TUs. Matching a storage account's default throughput would cost **~£333/mo** in TUs.
- **Storage scales without purchase** — 20,000 req/s and tens of Gbps by default, no unit to buy.
- At m7kni's volume (0.7 GB/mo ≈ **0.27 KB/s**) we are at **~0.03% of a single TU**. Neither is stressed; the question is academic here but **not** for the large-tenant intent, where blob scales for free and EH scales by invoice.

**Event Hub's genuine advantages are different: lower latency (push, no hourly batching) and built-in offset management** — which is exactly why [Microsoft steers SIEM tools to it](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/resource-logs-blob-format). Those are real. Scale is not one of them.

**A blob latency number on its own is uninterpretable.** If blob shows 40 min, that could be Entra's pipeline being slow *or* blob's hourly batching — opposite implications. Event Hub on the **same diagnostic setting, same events** decomposes it:

| result | meaning |

| EH ~2 min, blob ~40 min | batching is the cost. #106 may justify EH on latency. |
| EH ~20 min, blob ~25 min | latency is **Entra-side**. EH buys nothing, ever — for #89 **or** #106. |

**This cannot change #89's transport** (the cost gap is decisive regardless). Its value is entirely for **#106** — where Defender is near-real-time and the answer actually matters — and for the large-tenant polling-replacement intent.

## LIVE MEASUREMENTS — data arrived in ~15 min, not 24h. Three findings that change the design. (2026-07-16)

Diagnostic settings created ~12:33Z; **first data observed ~12:45Z**. The documented *"expect a delay of 24 hours before reporting data appears"* is **worst-case guidance, not a floor** — do not plan around it, but do not treat an empty container as broken either.

### 1. 🔴 The blob layout is NOT what Microsoft documents

Every published example shows `resourceId=/<ARM resource path>/y=/m=/d=/h=/m=00/PT1H.json`. The previous comment flagged the tenant-level form as **unverified**. It was, and it was **wrong**:

```
DOCUMENTED:  resourceId=/tenants/<tid>/providers/microsoft.aadiam/y=2026/m=07/d=16/h=12/m=00/PT1H.json
ACTUAL:      tenantId=4b8c18bd-2f9f-4227-af55-9f1061cf9c32/y=2026/m=07/d=16/h=12/m=00/PT1H.json
```

**Tenant-level (`microsoft.aadiam`) resources use a `tenantId=<guid>/` prefix, not `resourceId=`.** Container is `insights-logs-<categoryname-lowercased>`. Coding the consumer's prefix/listing logic to the docs would have produced a collector that finds nothing. Records inside are JSON Lines as documented.

### 2. 🔴 PAST-HOUR BLOBS KEEP GROWING — "closed hour" is not a safe concept

Maintainer spotted this from the arrival checker's output. Verified over a 90-second sample:

| blob | growth in 90s | hour closed |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `h=00` | **+8,489 b** | **13 hours earlier** |
| `h=11` | +144,075 b | 1 hour earlier |
| `h=12` | +219,424 b | current hour |

**A blob whose hour closed 13 hours ago was still being appended to.** Blobs are strictly partitioned by **event time** — verified by reading contents: `h=00` holds *only* events timestamped 00:xx (94 records, newest 00:52). So Azure is not misfiling; it is **backfilling history into the correct hour buckets** after the destination was created.

**Consequences:**

- **This retroactively vindicates dropping read-and-delete.** The original design was *"delete closed hours only, guarded by SafetyLag"*. That would have **destroyed data**: `h=00` looked safely closed for 13 hours while Azure was still writing to it. The £0.002/mo saving would have cost real records. Dropping delete was the right call for a reason nobody had identified at the time.
- **The consumer cannot walk forward and forget.** It must **re-check already-seen blobs for growth**, not just newer ones. `(blob, byte-offset)` checkpointing is still correct — a byte offset into an append blob is monotonic and stable — but the *"which blobs do I still need to watch, and for how long?"* question is now **open, with no obvious bound**.
- **Backfill on enablement is real and good news** — it means enabling the destination recovers history rather than starting from zero.

**Not yet understood:** only `h=00`, `h=11`, `h=12` exist — **no `h=01`–`h=10`**. The backfill mechanism, how far back it reaches, and when it stops are **unknown**. Do not guess; re-observe once settled.

### 3. ⚠️ Latency numbers so far are POLLUTED by backfill — do not quote them as steady-state

| path | min | median | max |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Blob** (event.time → blob write) | **5.6 min** | 14.1 min | 35.9 min |
| **Event Hub** (event.time → enqueued) | **3.1 min** | 24.0 min | **736.0 min** |

The 736-minute max is the 12-hour-old `h=00` backfill — proof the numbers are contaminated. **Median is meaningless while backfill runs.**

**`min` is the only defensible steady-state signal today: blob ~5.6 min vs Event Hub ~3.1 min.** If that holds after backfill settles, it lands in the **"latency is Entra-side; Event Hub buys ~2.5 minutes"** bucket — i.e. Event Hub would cost **£8.34/mo for ~2 minutes**, which would not justify it for #89 *or* #106. **That is a provisional read, not the verdict.** Re-measure on a clean window before deciding #106's transport.

### 4. ⚠️ Data-plane RBAC fails SILENTLY — the trap to document

Two separate instances, same class, both nearly misdiagnosed as "no data yet":

- **Blob:** `Owner` grants container list/create (control-plane actions) but **NOT** blob *content* read — that is a **DataAction**, needing `Storage Blob Data Reader`. Listing works, reading 403s.
- **Event Hub:** `Owner` grants `get_partition_properties` (management link) but **NOT** receive — needs **`Azure Event Hubs Data Receiver`**. **The SDK returned 0 events with NO error whatsoever.** The hub reported 262 events; the consumer read zero and reported success.

**This is the single most dangerous failure mode on this path**: it is indistinguishable from "the pipeline isn't working yet". `graph2otel-poller` already holds `Storage Blob Data Reader` (correct, and all it needs — read-and-delete is dropped). Any future Event Hub consumer needs `Azure Event Hubs Data Receiver` explicitly.

### Tooling: `g2o-arrival`

Installed for the maintainer at `~/.local/bin/g2o-arrival` (self-contained venv, `~/.local/share/g2o-arrival/`). Read-only, safe to run any time.

```

g2o-arrival --latency   # + propagation delay per path
```

Two real bugs were found and fixed writing it, both worth knowing for the consumer:
- `receive()`/`receive_batch()` **never return on their own** — `max_wait_time` only paces the callback. `PartitionContext` has **no `.close()`**. The client must be closed from **outside** the callback.
- `receive()` without a `partition_id` does **load-balancing that requires a checkpoint store** and takes >20s to claim partitions. Read **per-partition** to avoid it.

## VERDICT: Event Hub buys 12 seconds for £8.34/mo. **Blob only.** Tear the rig down. (2026-07-16 13:12Z)

First **clean, post-backfill** measurement. Window: events timestamped ≥ 13:00Z only, sampled at 13:12Z — the current hour, so no backfilled history contaminates it (backfill is filling `h=00`, `h=01`, `h=11`, `h=12`).

| path | newest record age | min latency | median latency |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Blob** | **4.6 min** | 4.4 min | 8.6 min |
| **Event Hub** | **4.4 min** | 3.6 min | 5.9 min |

### The finding: latency is Entra-side, not destination-side

**Both paths are floored at ~4 minutes**, and that floor is Microsoft's own pipeline — it exists *upstream of the destination*. Paying for a faster destination cannot buy back time that was spent before the fork.

**Event Hub's advantage on the metric that matters (how quickly the newest event is visible) is 12 seconds.** For **£8.34/mo** — 35–170x the entire pipeline it would serve.

Event Hub's median is genuinely better (5.9 vs 8.6 min) because it enqueues continuously while blob waits for batch flushes. **~2.7 minutes of median, against a SIEM whose other collectors poll on 15–60 minute cadences, is noise.**

**This is the pre-registered decision rule firing, not a post-hoc rationalisation.** The rule was written down before the data existed:

> *"EH ~20min, blob ~25min → latency is **Entra-side**. EH buys nothing, ever — for #89 **or** #106."*

That is the branch that fired, at a smaller absolute scale than guessed. Recording it that way so nobody later suspects the criterion was bent to fit the answer.

### Caveats — stated, not buried

- **12 minutes of one hour on a small tenant.** Under sustained high volume, blob batching could lag more than EH. Not measured.
- **Backfill was still running during the sample**, competing for throughput. That biases **against** blob, so the true steady-state gap is likely **smaller**, not larger. A point in blob's favour.
- **This does not fully settle #106.** Defender's streaming API may batch to storage differently than Entra diagnostic settings do. But the core finding — *the destination is not where latency lives* — is strong evidence that #106 should not buy an Event Hub namespace for latency reasons either. #106 should verify Defender's own blob write cadence before concluding, not inherit this number.

### Decision

**Blob only. Event Hub is closed for #89.** Combined with Phase 1, the transport wins on every criterion that was ever on the table:

| criterion | blob vs Event Hub |
| --- | --- |
| cost | **£0.05–0.24/mo vs £8.34/mo** (35–170x) |
| deletion | real + free vs **not expressible** (moot now — see the read-and-delete drop) |
| backfill | our config vs **1 day (Basic)** — and Azure backfills into blob on enablement |
| latency | **12 seconds slower.** That is the entire case for Event Hub. |
| #106 sharing | both can share; Log Analytics could not |

### 🔴 TEARDOWN REQUIRED — the rig is the only standing charge in this project

`graph2otel-latencytest` has served its purpose. Left running it costs **£8.32/mo**, versus ~£0.05–0.24/mo for everything else combined.

**Both steps are required** — deleting the namespace alone leaves a **dangling EH destination** on the diagnostic setting, which is exactly the mess this session cleaned four instances of:

```sh
# 1. re-PUT the aadiam setting WITHOUT eventHubAuthorizationRuleId (blob only)
# 2. az eventhubs namespace delete -n graph2otel-latencytest -g auditlogs
```

**Not yet torn down** — keeping it a short while to confirm the 4-minute floor holds across more than one hour, since that is the whole basis of this verdict and it rests on a 12-minute sample. Tear down once confirmed; it costs ~£0.27/day to keep.

### Bonus finding: backfill is progressive

`h=01` appeared **during** this measurement (hours present went `00, 11, 12` → `00, 01, 11, 12, 13`). Azure is progressively filling historical hour-buckets rather than doing one bulk dump. So the earlier "no `h=01`–`h=10`" puzzle is resolving on its own: **backfill walks forward and fills them in.**

This strengthens the backfill story — enabling the destination genuinely recovers history — and reinforces that **the consumer must re-check old blobs**, because a blob for a long-closed hour can appear or grow at any time.

An earlier comment excluded it, citing Microsoft's *"not essential for security investigations"* line. **That was wrong on two counts**, and the maintainer was right to push back.

**1. It is genuinely unreachable any other way — live-verified under the poller's own identity:**

**2. Microsoft's caveat is about ACTING on it, not collecting it.** The full quote warns against *"taking actions such as disabling applications based on this data, as doing so could cause misconfigurations and potential adverse effects such as **tenant lock-out**"*. That is advice not to **automate remediation** from it. graph2otel is a **SIEM feed** — it collects and never acts. Reading "not essential for security investigations" as "not worth collecting" conflated the two.

**Cost:** 21,554 rows / 0.009 GB per 7d → ~0.04 GB/mo → **~£0.0006/mo**. The volume objection ("generates a high volume of data") is real for a metrics pipeline and irrelevant for a log pipeline at this scale, capped by the 7-day lifecycle regardless.

**Shape note for the consumer:** this is service-to-service auth *within* the tenant (e.g. opening a Word document inside Teams), so `appId`/`appDisplayName` will be Microsoft first-party GUIDs, not tenant apps. Per the cardinality rule it is **log-shaped**: per-entity detail as log attributes, and any bounded aggregate (count by resource/result) gets a **log twin**, never a metric label keyed on the app.

## ⚠️ Correction: the "source must be mutually exclusive" statement here is WRONG — see #131

This issue records that `source: graph|blob` must be **mutually exclusive per collector**, because "both enabled = duplicate records". **That assumed dual-ship meant running the same signal twice.** It does not.

Maintainer clarification (2026-07-16):

> *"when I talk about dual ship I mean in the context of letting us get real time metrics from API polling but comprehensive log ingest via blob storage after we've built the shipper."*

The two routes are **complementary, not redundant** — split by **signal type**, not competing for one slot:

| mode | metrics from | logs from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `graph` (default, today) | Graph poll | Graph poll |
| `blob` | *(none, unless #128)* | blob |
| **`dual`** | **Graph poll** (fresh, no ~4-min floor) | **blob** (complete, no throttle, no beta dep) |

**There is no duplication**, because each route feeds a *different pipeline*. The duplication risk exists only if both emit into the **same** one — so `dual` must mean *"Graph stops emitting log twins; blob stops emitting metrics"*. That makes it a **mode**, not a source toggle, and it is a genuinely different design from what this issue assumed.

**Metrics want freshness; logs want completeness.** Dual-ship gives each the route that suits it, instead of forcing one compromise on both.

Design work moved to **#131**. Nothing here needs to change today — the blob consumer is unbuilt — but **do not implement `source` as an exclusive toggle on the strength of this issue's earlier statement.**


### Entra (17), grouped by why each earns its place

**No Graph route at all — blob is the ONLY source (2)**
`MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs` · `MicrosoftServicePrincipalSignInLogs`

**Sign-ins (4)** — 3 of these retire a **beta dependency** (`signInEventTypes` is beta-only, so `entra.signins.non_interactive` / `.service_principal` / `.managed_identity` are `Experimental`/opt-in today; diagnostic settings emit them as **first-class categories**, making them v1.0-stable and default-on-able).
`SignInLogs` (⏱ **latency instrument — REMOVE once measured**) · `NonInteractiveUserSignInLogs` · `ServicePrincipalSignInLogs` · `ManagedIdentitySignInLogs`

**Identity Protection (6)** — **3 have NO collector whatsoever**, and `UserRiskEvents` dodges the **1 req/s per-tenant IPC ceiling** (across all apps, no `Retry-After`) — graph2otel's tightest constraint.
`RiskyUsers` · `UserRiskEvents` · `RiskyServicePrincipals` · **`ServicePrincipalRiskEvents`** ❌no collector · **`RiskyAgents`** ❌no collector · **`AgentRiskEvents`** ❌no collector

**Dual-ship log side (2)** — covered by Graph today for *metrics*; blob supplies *logs*, per #131.
`AuditLogs` · `ProvisioningLogs`

**⚠️ Discovery — shape UNKNOWN (3)**
`GraphNotificationsActivityLogs` · `MicrosoftGraphPolicyLogs` · `PreAuthenticationDiscoveryLogs`
Absent from Microsoft's published category doc; the API returns no `categoryDisplayName`; no collector maps to them. **Nobody knows what these contain.** Enabled purely to observe — the same empiricism that caught the wrong blob prefix and the always-null `displayName` today. **Assess and then decide to keep or drop; do not leave them enabled unexamined.**

### Correction: the earlier exclusions were reasoned from a model that has since been overturned

An earlier comment excluded `AuditLogs`, `ProvisioningLogs`, and `UserRiskEvents` because *"shipped, working, non-beta Graph collectors already cover them — blob buys nothing today"*.

**That reasoning assumed sources are mutually exclusive.** The maintainer corrected that model (#131): under **dual-ship**, Graph supplies **real-time metrics** and blob supplies **comprehensive logs** — complementary, not competing. Graph covering the metric side is **not** a reason to skip blob for the log side. The exclusion is withdrawn.

### Deliberately still EXCLUDED (9) — with reasons, so this is not re-litigated

- `ADFSSignInLogs` — **zero rows**; no ADFS on this tenant
- `EnrichedOffice365AuditLogs` — **zero rows**; Sentinel-side ML enrichment that isn't running
- `NetworkAccessTrafficLogs`, `NetworkAccessAlerts`, `NetworkAccessConnectionEvents`, `NetworkAccessGenerativeAIInsights`, `RemoteNetworkHealthLogs` — **zero rows**; no Global Secure Access. (Note `NetworkAccessTrafficLogs` **does** have a Graph endpoint — #130 — so it was never the "no API" gap CLAUDE.md claimed.)
- `AzureADGraphActivityLogs` — deprecated, sunsetting API
- `B2CRequestLogs` — not a B2C tenant

### Intune (3)

`OperationalLogs` (confirmed no-Graph gap, #94) · `Devices` + `DeviceComplianceOrg` (**#132** — testing whether they carry per-device inventory; if `Devices` does, it retires the hourly full-fleet page-walk)

### Cost

All of it is **~£0.05–0.24/mo**, dominated by `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs` (~70% of volume). The Identity Protection categories emit **~zero** on m7kni until **#129** triggers a synthetic risk event. The 7-day lifecycle caps worst case. **No standing charge exists** — the Event Hub rig is torn down.

### The selection bar, for the record

**"No Graph route, or blob removes a beta dep, or blob supplies the log side of a dual-ship signal, or it is unassessed and cheap to observe."** Not "it exists" — nine categories were excluded on that basis.

## BUILT and live-verified — the consumer ships, `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs` is served (2026-07-16)

Commits: `fca3c08` (engine), `8027d10` (collector + wiring), `2b0f20c` (docs). `make check` green.

| piece | what |
| --- | --- |
| `internal/blobpipeline` | the engine: list → ranged read → parse JSON Lines → emit → advance a per-blob byte offset |
| `internal/blobpipeline/azblob_adapter.go` | the **only** file in graph2otel importing an Azure storage type; everything else depends on the `Source` interface, so the engine unit-tests offline against a fake |
| `checkpoint.BlobCursor` | `{blob name → bytes consumed}`, namespaced apart from window checkpoints on disk |
| `entra.graph_activity` | the collector — one OTLP log per Graph API call against the tenant |
| `blob_ingest.account_url` | one per-tenant config key. Setting it **is** the opt-in; unset registers no blob collectors at all |

### Live proof, against the real tenant

Ran the real binary (`otlp.protocol: stdout`, poller identity, scratch checkpoint dir):

```
cold start     7,993 records emitted, 8 blobs consumed, cursor persisted
restart            9 records emitted    <- no duplicates, no gaps
```

**The 9 were genuinely new**, and they landed via both growth paths in one run:

- `h=02` grew 4,976,340 → 4,991,559 — **a blob for an hour that closed 13 hours earlier**
- `h=14` grew 2,285,092 → 2,292,490 — the live hour

That is the acceptance bar met exactly: survives a restart without gaps or duplicates, and picks up a closed hour that grows.

### ⚠️ Correction: "a closed hour's blob keeps growing" was overstated

The earlier comment recorded *"'the hour is closed, this blob is final' is FALSE"* and left the re-check set as **"open, with no obvious bound"**. Re-measured on settled data, and the accurate model is narrower:

**Azure's enablement backfill walks history oldest-first, and an hour FREEZES once backfill passes it.**

| blob | 14:57 | 15:55 | state |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `h=00` | 326,636 b / 30 blocks | **unchanged** | frozen — backfill done with it |
| `h=01` | 2,443,626 b / 292 blocks | **unchanged** | frozen |
| `h=11`–`h=13` | — | **unchanged** | frozen |
| `h=02` | 4,035,436 b / 214 blocks | 5,002,133 b / 285 blocks | **backfill working on it now** |
| `h=03` | *did not exist* | 5,533 b / 1 block | **backfill just reached it** |
| `h=14` | 1,352,505 b | 2,381,705 b | current hour, normal |

So a "complete" state **does** exist. What does not exist is **any signal for when it is reached**, and it is not derivable from the clock — you cannot tell a frozen hour from one backfill has not started on.

**The design does not change**, and now rests on the accurate reason: byte-offset cursor (a watermark still cannot express this), re-check every seen blob (still no way to know which are done). But the cost story improves a lot — the re-check set is **not** unbounded, and in steady state **only 1–2 blobs actually grow per tick**, which the restart above measured: 2 of 8 blobs re-read, 9 records emitted, everything else a size comparison.

**Still open:** whether a frozen hour can *ever* grow again once enablement backfill is fully done. Not answerable while m7kni is still backfilling. The design is safe under both answers, so this is a curiosity, not a blocker — but do not assume either way.

### The append-op count — last cost unknown, settled, and Phase 1 was wrong

`append_blob_committed_block_count` is a direct count of billable AppendBlock ops (append blobs support no other write). Measured across the five **settled** hours (complete totals, backfill has passed them):

```
13,089,338 bytes over 1,237 appends  ->  247 appends/hour, ~10.6 KB per append
178,128 appends/month  ->  GBP 0.80/mo   (meter: GBP 0.0447 / 10K writes)
```

Phase 1 offered three scenarios and picked the wrong one:

| Phase 1 scenario | predicted | actual |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| 1 append/hour | £0.05/mo | |
| 1 append/minute ← *"most likely"* | £0.24/mo | |
| 1 append/event (worst case) | £2.96/mo | |
| **measured (~4 records/append)** | | **~£0.85/mo total** |

**The £0.05–0.24 range quoted throughout this issue is wrong — the real figure is ~£0.85/mo** (£0.80 appends + £0.04 listing at a 5m interval + ~£0.01 storage). Recording it rather than leaving the nicer number standing.

**It does not flip anything**: still ~10x cheaper than Event Hub (£8.34) and ~half of Log Analytics (£1.54), and Phase 1 explicitly pre-registered that *"even the worst case is roughly LA's price and 3x cheaper than EH Basic, so this uncertainty cannot flip the ranking"*. That held. But the estimate was 4x low, and the reason is worth keeping: Azure batches ~4 records per append, not ~1 per minute.

### Traps that cost real time, now pinned in code and `docs/blob-ingest.md`

Every one contradicts Microsoft's docs, and every one produces a **silently wrong** collector rather than an error:

1. **Prefix is `tenantId=<guid>/`, not `resourceId=/tenants/...`** — already known, now pinned. Coding to the docs lists zero blobs and reports success forever.
2. **`level` is `"Informational"` on EVERY record — including the 500s.** Verified across a 335-record sample spanning 200/201/204/400/401/403/404/500. Severity comes from `properties.responseStatusCode`; trusting `level` marks every server error INFO permanently. And `level` is a numeric string (`"4"`) on `SignInLogs` — so a severity mapper **shared across categories would be wrong twice over**.
3. **`durationMs` is a string (`"497815"`) at the top level and an int (`497815`) in `properties` — on the same record.** Bind to `properties` for every number.
4. **`azblob.NewClient` accepts a malformed URL** and fails only on the first request. `blob_ingest.account_url` is validated at startup instead, so a typo is one clear failure naming the value rather than a per-tick error on every blob collector.

### Acceptance criteria

- [x] Collector lands with per-entity detail as **log attributes**, never metric labels (#112) — it emits **no metrics at all**; deriving bounded aggregates is #128's question and is deliberately unanswered here
- [x] Live-verified end-to-end against the real tenant: rows in, OTLP out, consumed data acked
- [x] `docs/event-hub-fallback.md` updated to describe what was actually built — **renamed** to `docs/blob-ingest.md`; it opened with *"Status: design only. Nothing is provisioned, no collector code exists"* and described two rejected transports
- [x] README honest-scope updated — `MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs` moves from "confirmed permanent gap" to "served this way today"
- [x] `make check` green

**One honest qualification on "OTLP out":** verified through `telemetry.Emitter` to the stdout exporter, not pushed to Grafana Cloud. The OTLP exporter is shared with every shipped collector and nothing about it is blob-specific, so this is not a blob-shaped gap — but nothing has been enabled on camden, and that deploy is your call, not something to do behind your back.

### Closing this, with follow-ups filed

The mission was *"pick ONE fallback-ingest transport and build it"*. Transport chosen (Storage), evaluated against both alternatives with real meters, built, and live-verified on the signal that justified the whole path. Every acceptance box is ticked.

The remaining 16 Entra + 3 Intune categories are **more collectors on a now-built engine**, not more transport work — each is an `EndpointConfig`-shaped mapping, so they belong in their own issues rather than growing this one further. Filed separately.

Closing: every acceptance criterion is ticked. Transport chosen on real meters (Storage), both alternatives closed with reasons, consumer built and live-verified on the signal that justified the path.

Follow-ups carrying the rest, so nothing is lost:
- **#135** — the other 19 categories (mappings on the now-built engine, no transport work)
- **#131** — dual-ship mode; #128 — metrics from blob events; #129 — synthesise a risk event so the IPC mappings are verifiable
- **#132** / **#134** — blocked on blobs landing for those categories
- **#106** — can share this transport (Storage is a Defender streaming destination, Log Analytics is not), but must verify Defender's own blob write cadence rather than inherit #89's latency numbers

Two things deliberately NOT done: nothing is enabled on camden (that deploy is yours to call), and `SignInLogs` is still in the diagnostic setting as the latency instrument — it should be removed now that it has served its purpose.

## Final authoritative state (2026-07-17, #146)

For anyone who scrolled to the end instead of reading the body banner: **transport = Azure Storage blobs, consumer = `internal/blobpipeline`, read-only, byte-offset cursor, live in production, ~£0.85/mo measured.** The current reference is [`docs/blob-ingest.md`](../blob/main/docs/blob-ingest.md) — not this thread, and not `docs/event-hub-fallback.md` (deleted; superseded by what actually shipped, `2b0f20c`).

Reading guide for this 18-comment thread: it contains a five-layer correction chain (LA-favoured → Storage won; £0.05–0.24 → £0.85; "never settles" → hours freeze after backfill passes; "deletion mandatory" → read-only + lifecycle; "mutual exclusion wrong per #131" → #131 closed confirming mutual exclusion). Each superseded claim is corrected later in-thread or in the banner — trust the newest statement, and for anything load-bearing prefer the doc.

title: Research spike + build: pick ONE fallback-ingest transport — Log Analytics query-and-delete vs Event Hub pub/sub (evaluate cost + completeness first)

body:
## Summary

Every existing `logpipeline.WindowCollector` assumes one shape: a single paged `GET` with a
server- or client-side time-window `$filter`, drained via `nextLink`, watermarked on the
endpoint's own chronological field. Several signals identified across the epic's domain research
(M365 unified audit, Purview unified audit, and any future `/security/auditLog/queries`-shaped
API) use a fundamentally different shape:

1. `POST /security/auditLog/queries` — submit a query (`filterStartDateTime`,
   `filterEndDateTime`, `recordTypeFilters`, etc.), get back `{id, status: "notStarted"}`.
2. `GET /security/auditLog/queries/{id}` — poll until `status` is `succeeded` (also
   `running`/`failed`/`cancelled`).
3. `GET /security/auditLog/queries/{id}/records` — page the results once ready.

This is the single Graph API surface behind BOTH the M365 unified-audit collector and Purview's
unified-audit-event collector (same endpoint, different `recordTypeFilters`) — see `m365.md` §3a
and `purview.md` §3c. Building this once as a shared engine mode avoids two independent
collectors reimplementing create/poll/page/dedupe logic.

## What / why

Add a new mode to `internal/logpipeline` (or a sibling package, e.g. `internal/jobpipeline`) that:

- Submits the query job via a pluggable request-builder (workload-specific: the M365 collector
  submits Exchange/SharePoint/OneDrive/Teams `recordTypeFilters`; a future Purview collector
  submits Purview's).
- Polls `status` with backoff (no documented SLA in the fetched docs — start at ~30s, cap at
  ~4min per Microsoft's general long-running-operation guidance, and make the interval
  configurable since this is an assumption, not a confirmed number).
- Pages `records` via the existing `nextLink` draining logic once `succeeded`.
- Checkpoints on `filterEndDateTime` of the last successfully drained query (bounded rolling
  windows — e.g. advance a day/hour at a time), with per-record dedupe by `auditLogRecord.id`
  surviving reordering across result "blobs" (the polymorphic-blob architecture this API
  inherits conceptually from the old O365 Management Activity API's non-chronological content
  blobs — Graph's docs don't restate this caveat explicitly but the shape is the same).
- Hands drained records into the existing telemetry/checkpoint plumbing so downstream collectors
  don't need their own log-emission code.

## Scope

- New engine primitive only. No workload-specific collector logic (that's the M365/Purview
  collector issues, which depend on this).
- Must not regress or complicate any existing `WindowCollector` — this is additive.

## Feasibility + licensing notes

- `/security/auditLog/queries` is GA v1.0, not beta (confirmed via context7,
  `security-auditcoreroot-post-auditlogqueries.md`).
- No write scope required — same read-only posture as the rest of the project.
- The poll interval/backoff numbers are working assumptions pending live verification (see the
  paired spike issue below) — don't hardcode a number as if it were documented Microsoft SLA.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] New job-poll primitive lands in `internal/logpipeline` (or a clearly-named sibling package),
      with unit tests covering: submit → poll (pending/succeeded/failed/cancelled) → page → dedupe.
- [ ] Checkpoint scheme (window-end watermark + per-record ID dedupe) is documented in the
      package's doc comment, matching the pattern established by existing `WindowCollector`s.
- [ ] At least one existing test double / fake Graph server exercises the full submit→poll→page
      cycle including a `failed`/`cancelled` status path.
- [ ] `make check` green.

Part of #86.

comments.body: Closed by 6801985. `internal/jobpipeline` shipped: generic submit→poll(notStarted/running/succeeded/failed/cancelled, backoff)→page(nextLink)→dedupe(record id via shared checkpoint SeenIDs)→advance-watermark(to − SafetyLag), with create-side backoff for the rapid-submit 429 (#98). `JobCollector` implements `collector.WindowCollector`; real `JobClient` adapter over graphclient RawPost/RawGet. Sibling of logpipeline — the existing WindowCollector engine is untouched. Unit tests cover submit→poll→page→dedupe, failed/cancelled sentinels, and create-retry-then-succeed / give-up. `make check` green (-race). Confirmed live: `cancelled` is the real Graph `auditLogQueryStatus` wire value (British spelling). Unblocks #97.
